s23c-s110101-1-1.bodyHtml:
Most urinary tract infections (UTIs) are ascending: bowel flora colonise the periurethral area, enter the bladder through the urethra and can climb the ureter to the renal pelvis. Women are affected far more often because the urethra is short and close to the anus. Hematogenous seeding of the kidney is uncommon and points to Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia or candidemia.

Host factors

  • Urine flow is the main defence. Anything that causes stasis raises the risk: obstruction (stone, prostate enlargement, pregnancy-related ureteral dilation), neurogenic bladder, vesicoureteral reflux.
  • Foreign bodies: catheters carry biofilm, which protects organisms from antibiotics and host defences.
  • Sexual activity, spermicides and diaphragms change periurethral flora and inoculate the bladder.
  • Low estrogen after menopause lets vaginal lactobacilli fall and uropathogens colonise.
  • Diabetes: glycosuria, impaired neutrophil function and autonomic bladder dysfunction.

Organisms

OrganismSettingClue on the exam
Escherichia coliAbout three quarters of community UTIsLactose fermenter; P fimbriae bind uroepithelial glycolipids and favour pyelonephritis; type 1 fimbriae favour cystitis
Staphylococcus saprophyticusYoung, sexually active womenGram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant
Proteus mirabilisRecurrent or catheter UTI, stonesUrease splits urea to ammonia, alkaline urine (pH often above 7.5), struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) staghorn calculi; swarming motility
Klebsiella pneumoniaeHospital, diabetes, alcohol useMucoid, encapsulated lactose fermenter; urease positive
Enterococcus speciesCatheters, instrumentation, older menGram-positive cocci in chains; intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins
Pseudomonas aeruginosaCatheters, recent hospital careNon-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, grape-like odour, blue-green pigment

Urinalysis

Leukocyte esterase marks neutrophils (pyuria). The nitrite test turns positive when Enterobacterales reduce dietary nitrate to nitrite; it is often negative with Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus, which do not reduce nitrate, and when urine has sat in the bladder only briefly. White blood cell casts form only in renal tubules, so they place the infection (or inflammation) in the kidney.

Pathology of acute pyelonephritis

Grossly, the kidney is swollen with yellow cortical abscesses. Microscopically, neutrophils fill tubules and the interstitium while glomeruli are relatively spared. Complications include renal or perinephric abscess, papillary necrosis (diabetes, obstruction, sickle cell disease, analgesic use) and, in diabetes, emphysematous pyelonephritis with gas in the parenchyma.

Exam trap: casts mean kidney. Pyuria with bacteria but no casts fits cystitis; pyuria with white cell casts and fever fits pyelonephritis (or, without bacteria, interstitial nephritis).

Chronic and unusual infections

  • Chronic pyelonephritis: recurrent infection on a background of reflux or obstruction gives coarse, asymmetric corticomedullary scars over blunted calyces, most marked at the poles. Tubules fill with eosinophilic casts that resemble thyroid follicles ("thyroidization").
  • Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis: a destructive chronic infection, usually with an obstructing staghorn stone and Proteus or E. coli. Lipid-laden foamy macrophages form yellow masses that can mimic renal cell carcinoma; treatment is usually nephrectomy.
  • Genitourinary tuberculosis: hematogenous spread, often years after the primary infection. Classic clue: sterile pyuria (white cells, routine culture negative) with hematuria; caseating granulomas, calyceal distortion, ureteral strictures. Diagnose with acid-fast culture or nucleic acid testing of several first-morning urine samples.
  • Schistosoma haematobium: freshwater exposure in Africa or the Middle East; adult worms live in the vesical venous plexus, and eggs with a terminal spine lodge in the bladder wall. Terminal hematuria, granulomatous fibrosis, obstructive uropathy and, long term, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Treatment: praziquantel.
  • BK polyomavirus: reactivates in kidney transplant recipients on strong immunosuppression and causes tubulointerstitial nephritis with intranuclear inclusions ("decoy cells" in urine) and graft dysfunction. The main step is to reduce immunosuppression.
  • Adenovirus: hemorrhagic cystitis in children and transplant recipients.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Stones that smell of ammonia": urease producers (Proteus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Ureaplasma) make urine alkaline and build struvite.

s23c-s110102-1-1.bodyHtml:
The nephritic pattern comes from inflammation inside the glomerulus: leukocytes and proliferating cells injure capillary walls, so red cells leak into Bowman space. The result is hematuria with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, a fall in glomerular filtration (oliguria, azotemia), sodium and water retention with hypertension and edema, and proteinuria that is usually below the nephrotic range.

Where immune complexes sit decides how much inflammation they cause. Deposits on the blood side of the basement membrane (subendothelial, mesangial) are reached by complement and leukocytes and drive proliferation. Deposits on the urinary side (subepithelial) are shielded from circulating leukocytes and mainly injure podocytes, which gives proteinuria; the large subepithelial humps of post-infectious GN are the exception because they come with intense complement activation.

The main nephritic diseases

DiseaseImmunofluorescence and EMSerum complementClues
Post-streptococcal (post-infectious) GNGranular IgG and C3; large subepithelial humps; hypercellular glomeruli with neutrophilsLow C3, recovers in about 6–8 weeksLatent period: 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis, 3–6 weeks after impetigo; anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B; children usually recover fully
IgA nephropathyMesangial IgA (with C3); mesangial proliferationNormalGross hematuria within 1–3 days of a mucosal infection; galactose-deficient IgA1 and autoantibodies against it form complexes that lodge in the mesangium
IgA vasculitisSame renal lesion as IgA nephropathyNormalChild with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain (intussusception risk)
Anti-GBM diseaseLinear IgG along the GBM; crescentsNormalAutoantibody to the noncollagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen (type II hypersensitivity); lung involvement gives alveolar hemorrhage
ANCA-associated (pauci-immune) GNLittle or no immunoglobulin or complement; necrotising lesions with crescentsNormalGranulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA; sinus and lung disease), microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA; no granulomas), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (asthma, eosinophilia)
Lupus nephritis (classes III, IV)"Full house" IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q; subendothelial deposits thicken capillary loops ("wire loops")Low C3 and C4Anti-dsDNA titres and low complement track activity; class IV (diffuse) is the most common severe form
Immune-complex MPGNSubendothelial and mesangial deposits; GBM duplicated by interposed mesangium ("tram-track")Low C3 (and often C4)Chronic antigenemia: hepatitis C (often with mixed cryoglobulins), hepatitis B, endocarditis, monoclonal gammopathy
C3 glomerulopathy (including dense deposit disease)C3 alone, little immunoglobulinLow C3, normal C4Dysregulated alternative pathway, for example C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilises the C3 convertase C3bBb
Cryoglobulinemic GNIntraluminal "thrombi" of cryoglobulin; MPGN patternVery low C4Hepatitis C, palpable purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy, positive rheumatoid factor

Lupus nephritis classes

  • I minimal mesangial and II mesangial proliferative: mild, usually hematuria or low-grade proteinuria.
  • III focal (fewer than half of glomeruli) and IV diffuse (half or more) proliferative: subendothelial deposits, active sediment, hypertension, falling GFR; need immunosuppression.
  • V membranous: subepithelial deposits, nephrotic syndrome; may coexist with III or IV.
  • VI advanced sclerosing: 90% or more of glomeruli scarred; treat as CKD.

Rapidly progressive GN

Any of the above can form crescents: fibrin leaks through ruptured capillary walls into Bowman space and provokes proliferation of parietal epithelial cells with macrophages. Crescents in most glomeruli mean kidney function falls over days to weeks. Immunofluorescence sorts crescentic GN into three groups: linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune complex: lupus, IgA, post-infectious) and pauci-immune (ANCA).

Hereditary basement-membrane disease

  • Alport syndrome: abnormal type IV collagen (most often X-linked COL4A5, alpha-5 chain). Hematuria from childhood, then proteinuria and progressive CKD in affected males, with sensorineural hearing loss and eye changes (anterior lenticonus). EM shows an irregularly thickened, thinned and split ("basket-weave") GBM. Anti-GBM disease can appear in a transplanted kidney because the graft carries collagen the recipient never made.
  • Thin basement membrane nephropathy: often a heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 variant; persistent microscopic hematuria with a uniformly thin GBM and usually preserved function, although some patients progress, so they are followed.

Exam trap: timing separates IgA nephropathy from post-streptococcal GN. Hematuria during or a day or two after the sore throat, with normal C3, is IgA nephropathy; hematuria 2 or more weeks later with low C3 is post-infectious GN.

Memory aid (Naadi): complement tells you who is consuming it. Low C3 and C4 together: immune complexes on the classical pathway (lupus, cryoglobulins, immune-complex MPGN). Low C3 with normal C4: the alternative pathway (post-infectious GN, C3 glomerulopathy). Normal complement: IgA, anti-GBM, ANCA.

s23c-s110102-1-2.bodyHtml:
The nephrotic syndrome is podocyte or filtration-barrier injury without much inflammation: proteinuria above 3.5 g/day in adults, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (oval fat bodies and fatty casts that show "Maltese crosses" under polarised light). The sediment is otherwise bland.

Consequences of heavy proteinuria

  • Edema: low oncotic pressure plus primary renal sodium retention in the collecting duct.
  • Hyperlipidemia: the liver raises lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, and lipoprotein clearance falls.
  • Hypercoagulability: urinary loss of antithrombin (and proteins C and S) while the liver makes more fibrinogen and other clotting factors. Venous thrombosis, including renal vein thrombosis, is most common with membranous nephropathy.
  • Infection: urinary loss of IgG and complement factors; children are prone to spontaneous peritonitis and cellulitis, classically with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
  • Loss of binding proteins: low total thyroxine and 25-hydroxyvitamin D with normal free hormone in many patients.

The main nephrotic diseases

DiseaseLight microscopyIF and EMAssociations
Minimal change diseaseNormalIF negative; EM: diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processesMost common cause in young children; highly steroid responsive; in adults NSAIDs and Hodgkin lymphoma; autoantibodies to the podocyte protein nephrin have been found in many patients
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)Scarring of part of some glomeruliIF usually negative (nonspecific IgM, C3 in scars); effacementCommon cause in adults, especially Black adults (two APOL1 risk variants); secondary forms: HIV (collapsing variant), heroin, obesity, sickle cell disease, reduced nephron mass, lithium, pamidronate; less steroid responsive
Membranous nephropathyDiffusely thickened capillary wallsGranular IgG and C3; subepithelial deposits with intervening basement-membrane "spikes" on silver stainCommon cause in older adults; about 70–80% of primary cases have antibodies to the podocyte phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R); secondary: lupus class V, hepatitis B, solid tumours, NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine
Diabetic nephropathyMesangial expansion, GBM thickening, nodular sclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), hyaline arteriolosclerosis of both afferent and efferent arteriolesLinear, nonspecific IgG along the GBMHyperfiltration early: glomerular capillary pressure rises because angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole
AmyloidosisAcellular, amorphous mesangial and capillary depositsCongo red stain with apple-green birefringence under polarised light; random 8–12 nm fibrils on EMAL (light chains from a plasma cell clone) or AA (serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation: rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, familial Mediterranean fever, chronic infection)

Acute interstitial nephritis

Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is inflammation of the interstitium and tubules, not the glomerulus. Most cases are a drug reaction mediated mainly by T cells (type IV hypersensitivity): beta-lactams, sulfonamides, rifampin, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors are frequent culprits. Onset is usually days to weeks after the drug starts (sooner on re-exposure; months with NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors). Features: rising creatinine, sterile pyuria and white cell casts, mild proteinuria, and sometimes fever, rash and eosinophilia (the full triad is uncommon). Biopsy shows interstitial edema with lymphocytes, plasma cells and often eosinophils. Other causes are infections and systemic disease (sarcoidosis, Sjögren syndrome, IgG4-related disease).

Exam trap: NSAIDs can cause minimal change disease (or membranous nephropathy) and interstitial nephritis at the same time, so heavy proteinuria with pyuria after long NSAID use does not need two diagnoses.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Normal under the light, flat under the beam": minimal change looks normal by light microscopy and shows only flattened foot processes under the electron beam.

s23c-s110201-1-1.bodyHtml:
Renal cysts range from the trivial (a simple cyst found on a scan for something else) to inherited diseases that end in kidney failure. Benign solid tumours of the kidney matter mostly because they can look like cancer. Sort them by pattern (one cyst or many, cortex or medulla), kidney size and inheritance.

Simple cysts

Fluid-filled, thin-walled cysts lined by a single layer of flattened epithelium. They become more common with age and are present in a large share of adults over 50. They are usually silent; rarely they bleed, become infected or are large enough to cause pain. A cyst with thick walls, septa, calcification or enhancing tissue is complex and needs a different approach (see Step 2 CK).

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

  • Genetics: PKD1 on chromosome 16 (about 80% of families; more severe, earlier kidney failure) or PKD2 on chromosome 4 (milder). The proteins, polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, sit in the primary cilium of tubular cells and regulate calcium entry. A second, somatic hit in the normal allele of a single tubular cell starts each cyst, so cysts appear over decades rather than at birth.
  • Cyst growth: low intracellular calcium raises cAMP, which drives epithelial proliferation and chloride-driven fluid secretion into the cyst (through CFTR). Vasopressin acting on V2 receptors in the collecting duct is a major source of that cAMP, which is why the V2 antagonist tolvaptan slows kidney growth.
  • Kidneys: both enlarge massively, replaced by cysts from every part of the nephron. Expanding cysts compress intrarenal vessels, causing local ischemia, renin-angiotensin activation and early hypertension, often before the GFR falls.
  • Renal features: flank pain, gross hematuria from cyst rupture, cyst infection, calcium oxalate and uric acid stones, a urinary concentrating defect, and progressive CKD that usually reaches kidney failure in middle age with PKD1.
  • Extrarenal features: liver cysts (the commonest; larger and more common in women with estrogen exposure), saccular (berry) aneurysms of the circle of Willis (risk clusters in families), mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, abdominal and inguinal hernias, pancreatic and seminal vesicle cysts.

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)

Mutations in PKHD1 (fibrocystin, also a ciliary protein). The collecting ducts dilate into cysts arranged radially from medulla to cortex, so both kidneys are large and echogenic from fetal life. Poor fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios and the Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, limb deformities); pulmonary hypoplasia is the main cause of neonatal death. Every child also has congenital hepatic fibrosis (ductal plate malformation), which causes portal hypertension and cholangitis in survivors.

Other cystic kidneys

ConditionKidney sizeKey points
Acquired cystic kidney diseaseSmall, scarredDevelops with long-standing kidney failure, especially on dialysis; cysts can bleed; renal cell carcinoma risk is raised
Medullary sponge kidneyNormalDilated medullary (inner) collecting ducts, usually sporadic; calcium stones, nephrocalcinosis, UTIs and hematuria in young adults; urography shows linear streaks of contrast in the papillae; kidney function is usually preserved
Nephronophthisis (autosomal recessive)Small or normalCorticomedullary cysts with tubulointerstitial fibrosis; polyuria and salt wasting in childhood, kidney failure in the teens
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney diseaseSmall or normalAdult-onset CKD with bland urine; UMOD variants cause early gout

Benign solid tumours

  • Angiomyolipoma: a benign tumour of perivascular epithelioid cells made of three tissues: mature fat, smooth muscle and thick-walled blood vessels. Most are sporadic and solitary; multiple, bilateral tumours suggest tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1 hamartin or TSC2 tuberin, which normally restrain mTORC1). The abnormal vessels lack normal elastic tissue and form aneurysms, so large tumours can bleed into the retroperitoneum. Macroscopic fat on CT is the imaging signature. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink TSC-related tumours. Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis belongs to the same tumour family.
  • Oncocytoma: a benign tumour from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Large cells with granular pink cytoplasm, packed with mitochondria; grossly mahogany-brown with a central stellate scar. It cannot be reliably told apart from carcinoma on imaging, so it is often removed.
  • Papillary adenoma: tiny (15 mm or less) low-grade papillary tumours of the cortex found incidentally; common in scarred kidneys.

Exam trap: large kidneys with many cysts and hypertension in an adult is ADPKD; small kidneys with many cysts in someone on dialysis is acquired cystic disease. Size tells them apart, and the second carries a cancer risk.

Memory aid (Naadi): the angiomyolipoma name lists its own recipe: angio (vessels), myo (smooth muscle), lipoma (fat).

s23c-s110202-1-1.bodyHtml:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)

RCC arises from renal tubular epithelium and is the main primary kidney cancer of adults, peaking in the sixth and seventh decades and more common in men. Risk factors: smoking (the strongest modifiable one), obesity, hypertension, acquired cystic kidney disease of dialysis, and inherited syndromes, chiefly von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease.

SubtypeShareOrigin and geneticsMicroscopy
Clear cellAbout 70–75%Proximal tubule; loss of chromosome 3p and inactivation of VHL (sporadic or inherited)Cells with clear cytoplasm (glycogen and lipid washed out in processing) in nests with a delicate, richly vascular network
PapillaryAbout 10–15%Proximal tubule; trisomy 7 and 17; hereditary form with activating MET mutations; common in acquired cystic diseasePapillae with foamy macrophages in the cores, psammoma bodies
ChromophobeAbout 5%Intercalated cells; multiple whole-chromosome lossesPale cells with prominent cell borders and perinuclear halos; better prognosis
Collecting duct and medullaryRareCollecting duct; medullary carcinoma occurs in young people with sickle cell traitAggressive, infiltrative

VHL and the hypoxia pathway

The VHL protein is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) for destruction when oxygen is present. When both copies are lost (two hits, as for any tumour suppressor), HIF accumulates even in normal oxygen and switches on VEGF, PDGF, erythropoietin and glucose transporter genes. That explains the vascularity of clear cell RCC and why drugs that block VEGF signalling work. VHL disease (autosomal dominant) causes bilateral, multifocal clear cell RCC and renal cysts at a young age, cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

Clinical behaviour

  • Most tumours are now found incidentally on imaging. The classic triad of hematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass is uncommon and usually means advanced disease.
  • RCC grows into the renal vein and can extend up the inferior vena cava to the right atrium. A left varicocele that does not empty when the patient lies down suggests obstruction of the left gonadal vein where it joins the left renal vein.
  • Spread is hematogenous: lung ("cannonball" nodules), bone (purely lytic lesions), liver and brain.
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes are common: erythropoietin (polycythemia), PTH-related peptide (hypercalcemia with low PTH), renin (hypertension), ACTH (Cushing syndrome), fever and weight loss, and a reversible cholestatic liver dysfunction without metastases (Stauffer syndrome).

Drugs used against RCC (by mechanism)

  • VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sunitinib, pazopanib, axitinib, cabozantinib): adverse effects include hypertension, proteinuria, hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhea, hypothyroidism and impaired wound healing.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors: anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) release T-cell brakes; adverse effects are immune-mediated (colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenalitis, type 1 diabetes).
  • mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus) and the HIF-2α inhibitor belzutifan (used for VHL-associated tumours).
  • RCC is resistant to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy.

Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)

The commonest primary kidney cancer of children, usually between 2 and 5 years. It arises from persistent metanephric blastema (nephrogenic rests) and shows a triphasic pattern: small round blue blastemal cells, primitive tubules and glomeruloid structures (epithelium), and spindle-cell stroma. It presents as a large, smooth, unilateral flank mass that rarely crosses the midline, sometimes with hematuria, abdominal pain or hypertension (renin). Lung is the usual site of metastasis. Unfavourable (anaplastic) histology carries TP53 mutations.

SyndromeGeneticsFeatures
WAGRDeletion at 11p13 including WT1 and PAX6Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability (range of developmental delay)
Denys-DrashDominant-negative WT1 point mutationEarly nephrotic syndrome with diffuse mesangial sclerosis, disorders of sex development, Wilms tumour
Beckwith-WiedemannImprinting defects at 11p15.5 (for example overexpression of IGF2)Macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, lateralised overgrowth (hemihypertrophy), neonatal hypoglycemia; Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma

Neuroblastoma, the other big abdominal tumour of young children, arises from the adrenal medulla, is often calcified, crosses the midline and raises urine catecholamine metabolites; Wilms tumour does none of these.

Urothelial carcinoma

The urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and proximal urethra, and carcinogens excreted in urine expose all of it at once. Tumours are often multifocal and recur (a "field effect"). Most arise in the bladder; upper-tract tumours are less common.

  • Risk factors: cigarette smoking (the leading cause); occupational aromatic amines (benzidine, 2-naphthylamine in dye, rubber and leather work); cyclophosphamide (its metabolite acrolein also causes hemorrhagic cystitis, prevented by hydration and mesna); long-term phenacetin-containing analgesics (papillary necrosis and renal pelvis tumours); aristolochic acid (some herbal remedies; upper-tract tumours); pelvic radiation. Lynch syndrome raises the risk of upper-tract tumours.
  • Two pathways: low-grade papillary tumours recur often but rarely invade; flat carcinoma in situ and high-grade tumours tend to invade. Stage depends on depth: invasion of the muscularis propria separates non-muscle-invasive from muscle-invasive disease and is the key prognostic step.
  • Presentation: painless gross hematuria; irritative voiding symptoms with carcinoma in situ.
  • Intravesical BCG (live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis) treats high-grade non-muscle-invasive tumours and carcinoma in situ by provoking a local Th1-type immune response that kills tumour cells.

Other bladder cancers

  • Squamous cell carcinoma: chronic irritation and squamous metaplasia: Schistosoma haematobium, long-term catheters, chronic stones.
  • Adenocarcinoma: urachal remnant at the bladder dome, bladder exstrophy, glandular metaplasia.

Exam trap: painless gross hematuria in an older smoker is urothelial cancer until proved otherwise, even if he is taking an anticoagulant or the bleeding stops.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Three-p, pee clear": loss of chromosome 3p gives clear cell carcinoma of the kidney.

s23c-s110301-1-1.bodyHtml:
A urine sample is a liquid biopsy of the kidney. Three parts are read together: the dipstick (chemistry), microscopy of the spun sediment, and the volume and colour. Each answers a different question, and each has blind spots.

The dipstick and its blind spots

PadWhat it detectsMisses or misleads
ProteinMainly albumin (negatively charged)Light chains and other low-molecular-weight proteins; very alkaline or concentrated urine gives false positives
Blood (heme)Peroxidase activity of hemoglobin and myoglobinPositive with free hemoglobin or myoglobin and no red cells: always confirm with microscopy
GlucoseGlucose onlyPositive when the filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorption (threshold about 180 mg/dL in plasma), or with an SGLT2 inhibitor, pregnancy or proximal tubule damage at normal plasma glucose
Leukocyte esterase, nitriteNeutrophils; nitrate-reducing gram-negative bacteriaSee urinary infections
Specific gravityConcentration (roughly tracks osmolality)Raised by glucose, contrast and protein beyond their osmotic effect
Bilirubin, urobilinogenConjugated bilirubin; urobilinogenConjugated bilirubin in urine means cholestasis or hepatocellular disease; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin bound and never appears

Hematuria: where is the blood coming from?

Glomerular bleeding forces red cells through gaps in the glomerular basement membrane and then through the osmotic and pH changes of the tubule, so they arrive dysmorphic (blebbed ring forms called acanthocytes), often with red cell casts and proteinuria, and the urine is brown or "cola" coloured. Nonglomerular bleeding (stones, tumours, infection, prostate, papillary necrosis) gives uniform, round red cells, sometimes clots, and usually no significant proteinuria. Clots argue strongly against a glomerular source, because urokinase in tubular fluid lyses glomerular blood.

Heme-positive dipstick without red cells means a pigment:

  • Myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis: crush injury, prolonged immobility, extreme exertion, statins with interacting drugs, seizures): small (about 17 kDa), freely filtered and cleared, so plasma stays clear; creatine kinase is very high. Myoglobin is toxic to tubules and causes acute tubular necrosis.
  • Hemoglobin (intravascular hemolysis): plasma is pink, haptoglobin is low and LDH and indirect bilirubin are high.

Papillary necrosis gives painless or colicky hematuria; remember its causes: diabetes, analgesic overuse, sickle cell disease or trait, obstruction with infection, and severe pyelonephritis. In sickle cell trait the hypertonic, hypoxic renal medulla promotes sickling, so painless hematuria and an inability to concentrate urine (isosthenuria) can occur even in carriers; renal medullary carcinoma is a rare, aggressive tumour of young people with sickle trait.

Proteinuria: how much and what kind?

Normal excretion is below 150 mg of protein and below 30 mg of albumin a day; much of the normal protein is Tamm-Horsfall glycoprotein (uromodulin) secreted by the thick ascending limb. Spot ratios estimate daily excretion: the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR, mg/g) and protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR, g/g are roughly g/day).

TypeMechanismTypical amount and clue
GlomerularLoss of the size or charge barrier lets albumin throughAlbumin-dominant; above 3.5 g/day is nephrotic range
TubularProximal tubule fails to reabsorb filtered small proteins (beta-2 microglobulin, retinol-binding protein)Usually below 2 g/day; dipstick often weakly positive or negative; Fanconi syndrome, heavy metals, interstitial nephritis
OverflowPlasma excess of a small protein exceeds tubular uptakeImmunoglobulin light chains in myeloma (dipstick negative, UPCR high); myoglobin; hemoglobin
Functional or transientAltered glomerular hemodynamicsFever, intense exercise, heart failure, seizures; usually below 1 g/day and gone on repeat
OrthostaticIncreased protein excretion when uprightAdolescents and young adults, below about 1 g/day, absent in a first-morning sample; benign

Exam trap: a negative or trace dipstick with a high UPCR (or a positive sulfosalicylic acid test) means the protein is not albumin. Think light chains and look for anemia, hypercalcemia and renal failure.

Microscopy: casts and crystals

Casts are cylinders of Tamm-Horsfall protein moulded in the distal tubule and collecting duct, so anything trapped in a cast came from the kidney.

Crystals: calcium oxalate dihydrate looks like envelopes (monohydrate needles or dumbbells suggest ethylene glycol), uric acid forms rhomboids or rosettes in acid urine, struvite forms "coffin lids" in alkaline infected urine, and cystine forms hexagons, which are always abnormal.

Urine colour

ColourCauses
Red or pinkRed cells, hemoglobin, myoglobin, beets (in some people), rifampin (orange-red), porphyrins
OrangePhenazopyridine, rifampin, concentrated urine, conjugated bilirubin
Brown or colaGlomerular bleeding, myoglobin, conjugated bilirubin, metronidazole
Darkens to black on standingAlkaptonuria (homogentisic acid oxidises; ochronosis of cartilage); also melanuria with metastatic melanoma
Port-wine, darkening in lightPorphyrias (acute intermittent porphyria during attacks)
Green or blueMethylene blue, propofol, amitriptyline, Pseudomonas
MilkyPyuria, phosphate crystals, chyluria (lymphatic fistula, filariasis)

Abnormal volume

  • Oliguria is below about 400 mL/day (or below 0.5 mL/kg/h); anuria is below about 100 mL/day. True anuria is unusual and points to complete obstruction (including a blocked catheter), bilateral renal arterial or venous occlusion, cortical necrosis or severe rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
  • Polyuria is above about 3 L/day. The urine osmolality separates a water diuresis (urine osmolality well below plasma, usually below about 250 mOsm/kg: central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, primary polydipsia) from a solute diuresis (urine osmolality near or above plasma, about 300 mOsm/kg or more: glucose, urea after relief of obstruction or high-protein feeding, mannitol, saline).

Naadi memory aid: "Dip, spin, look": dip for chemistry, spin for the sediment, look at the colour and volume. A finding counts only when all three agree.

s23c-s110401-1-1.bodyHtml:
Glomerular filtration

The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is set by the Starling forces across the glomerular capillary: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, and Bowman space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure oppose it. Because the glomerular capillary bed sits between two arterioles, their tone controls the pressure inside it.

ChangeRenal plasma flow (RPF)GFRFiltration fraction (GFR/RPF)Example
Afferent constrictionDownDownAbout unchangedNSAIDs (loss of prostaglandin dilation), sympathetic tone
Afferent dilationUpUpAbout unchangedProstaglandins, high-protein meal
Efferent constrictionDownUp (modest)UpAngiotensin II in volume depletion
Efferent dilationUpDownDownACE inhibitors, ARBs
Higher plasma oncotic pressureNo changeDownDownMultiple myeloma paraproteins, dehydration
Ureteral obstructionNo changeDownDownRaised Bowman space pressure

The normal filtration fraction is about 20%. Prerenal states lean on efferent constriction by angiotensin II and on afferent dilation by prostaglandins to hold GFR up, which is why an ACE inhibitor or an NSAID can tip a volume-depleted patient into acute kidney injury.

Clearance

Clearance is the plasma volume cleared of a substance per minute: C = (U × V) / P, where U is urine concentration, V urine flow and P plasma concentration.

  • Inulin is filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR.
  • Creatinine is filtered and slightly secreted, so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR. Drugs that block creatinine secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine) raise serum creatinine without changing true GFR.
  • Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is filtered and almost completely secreted, so its clearance estimates effective renal plasma flow. Renal blood flow = RPF / (1 − hematocrit).
  • A substance with clearance below the GFR is net reabsorbed (glucose, sodium, urea); above the GFR, net secreted.

Serum creatinine rises late: the relationship between creatinine and GFR is hyperbolic, so losing half the GFR from normal only moves creatinine from about 0.8 to 1.6 mg/dL. Cystatin C is less affected by muscle mass and is used to confirm an estimated GFR.

Segment by segment

SegmentKey transporters and functionsDrug or disease at this site
Proximal tubuleAbout two thirds of filtered sodium and water; NaHCO₃ via carbonic anhydrase and Na⁺/H⁺ exchange; glucose by SGLT2; amino acids, phosphate, urate; ammoniagenesis from glutamine; organic acid and base secretionAcetazolamide, SGLT2 inhibitors; Fanconi syndrome, type 2 RTA, cystinuria
Thin descending limbWater leaves into the hypertonic medullaMannitol (osmotic, acts mainly here and in the proximal tubule)
Thick ascending limbNKCC2 (Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻); K⁺ recycling through ROMK creates a lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ uptake; water-impermeable ("diluting segment")Loop diuretics; Bartter syndrome
Distal convoluted tubuleNCC (Na⁺-Cl⁻); PTH-regulated Ca²⁺ reabsorptionThiazides (lower urine calcium); Gitelman syndrome
Collecting duct, principal cellENaC sodium uptake and ROMK potassium secretion under aldosterone; aquaporin-2 inserted by ADH via V2 receptorsAmiloride, triamterene, mineralocorticoid antagonists; Liddle syndrome; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Collecting duct, α-intercalated cellH⁺-ATPase and H⁺/K⁺-ATPase secrete acid; urine buffered as NH₄⁺ and titratable acidType 1 RTA

Exam trap: a rise in creatinine of up to about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB is expected (efferent dilation) and is not a reason to stop it; a larger rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Loops lose calcium, thiazides keep it": loop diuretics raise urine calcium (useful in hypercalcemia), thiazides lower it (useful in calcium stones).

s23c-s110401-1-2.bodyHtml:
Acute kidney injury (AKI)

AKI is a fall in kidney function over hours to days. Think of it by where the problem lies.

FeaturePrerenalIntrinsic: acute tubular necrosisPostrenal
MechanismLow effective perfusion; tubules intact and avidly reabsorb sodium and waterTubular cells die and slough; casts obstruct tubules; filtrate leaks backObstruction raises tubular and Bowman pressure
BUN:creatinineAbove 2010–15Variable (often above 15 early)
Urine sodiumBelow 20 mEq/LAbove 40 mEq/LVariable
FENaBelow 1%Above 2%Variable
Urine osmolalityAbove 500 mOsm/kgClose to plasma (about 300)Variable
SedimentBland, hyaline castsMuddy brown granular and renal tubular epithelial cell castsBland; hydronephrosis on ultrasound

FENa = (urine Na × plasma Cr) / (plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100. Diuretics raise FENa even in prerenal states; the fractional excretion of urea (below about 35% in prerenal AKI) is less affected.

Acute tubular necrosis

  • Ischemic ATN follows prolonged hypotension or shock. The straight part of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb are most vulnerable, because they work hard in an area that receives little oxygen. Injury is patchy.
  • Nephrotoxic ATN mainly damages the proximal tubule: aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, iodinated contrast, and pigments (myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobin in hemolysis).
  • Rhabdomyolysis: crush injury, prolonged immobility, extreme exertion, statins, seizures. The dipstick is positive for blood but few red cells are seen, because the dipstick detects heme in myoglobin. Creatine kinase is very high; potassium and phosphate rise, calcium falls early.
  • Tumor lysis: after cytotoxic therapy of bulky, fast-growing tumours (Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemia). Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystallise in tubules. Labs: high potassium, phosphate and uric acid, low calcium.
  • Course: initiation, a maintenance phase with oliguria and hyperkalemia, then a recovery phase with polyuria in which hypokalemia and volume depletion are risks.

Chronic kidney disease (CKD)

CKD is kidney damage or GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for more than 3 months. The most common causes are diabetes and hypertension. Once nephrons are lost, the survivors hyperfilter; the raised glomerular pressure injures them in turn (adaptive hyperfiltration), driving progressive glomerulosclerosis.

  • Anemia: normocytic, from low erythropoietin made by peritubular interstitial cells, plus iron deficiency and inflammation.
  • CKD-mineral and bone disorder: phosphate retention and high FGF23 lower 1α-hydroxylase activity, so calcitriol falls; calcium falls, and secondary hyperparathyroidism follows. Bone disease (renal osteodystrophy, including osteitis fibrosa cystica) and vascular calcification result. After years, parathyroid glands can become autonomous: tertiary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia, often unmasked after transplant.
  • Metabolic acidosis: falling ammoniagenesis; first with a normal anion gap, later with a raised gap from retained sulfate, phosphate and urate.
  • Hyperkalemia, salt and water retention, hypertension.
  • Uremia: nausea, anorexia, pruritus, pericarditis, encephalopathy (asterixis), platelet dysfunction with bleeding, peripheral neuropathy.

Hypertensive renal disease

  • Benign nephrosclerosis (long-standing hypertension): hyaline arteriolosclerosis narrows afferent arterioles; patchy ischemic glomerulosclerosis; small kidneys with a finely granular surface. Diabetes produces the same hyaline change.
  • Hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension): hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (concentric "onion-skin" smooth muscle and basement membrane layers) and fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles; petechial cortical hemorrhages ("flea-bitten" kidney); AKI with hematuria and microangiopathic hemolysis.

Low effective perfusion; tubules intact and avidly reabsorb sodium and water
Tubular cells die and slough; casts obstruct tubules; filtrate leaks back
Obstruction raises tubular and Bowman pressure

FENa = (urine Na × plasma Cr) / (plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100. Diuretics raise FENa even in prerenal states; the fractional excretion of urea (below about 35% in prerenal AKI) is less affected.
ATN follows prolonged hypotension or shock. The
straight part of the proximal tubule
and the medullary thick ascending limb are most vulnerable, because they work hard in an area that receives little oxygen. Injury is patchy.
ATN mainly damages the proximal tubule: aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, iodinated contrast, and pigments (myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobin in hemolysis).

CKD is kidney damage or GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for more than 3 months. The most common causes are diabetes and hypertension. Enteric hyperoxaluria: with fat malabsorption (Crohn disease, ileal resection, bariatric surgery), unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in the gut lumen. Oxalate that would have left as insoluble calcium oxalate stays free, and the colon absorbs it, raising urine oxalate. A normal calcium intake taken with meals protects; restricting calcium makes oxalate stones worse.

Renal tubular acidosis (RTA)

RTA causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis from the kidney. The urine anion gap (Na⁺ + K⁺ − Cl⁻) estimates urine ammonium: negative when the kidney excretes ammonium normally (as in diarrhea), positive when ammonium excretion is impaired (types 1 and 4).

Fanconi syndrome

Generalised failure of the proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate and urate are lost in urine. Clues are glycosuria with a normal blood glucose, hypophosphatemia (rickets or osteomalacia), hypouricemia and a type 2 RTA. Causes: tenofovir, ifosfamide, expired tetracycline, light-chain injury in multiple myeloma, Wilson disease, lead and other heavy metals, and in children cystinosis.

Cystinuria

An autosomal recessive defect of the apical transporter for dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine) in the proximal tubule and intestine. Only cystine, which is poorly soluble in acidic urine, forms stones. It is a transport disorder, distinct from cystinosis, a lysosomal storage disease.

DisorderDefectBlood pressureLabs

Liddle syndromeGain of function in ENaC (autosomal dominant)HighHypokalemia, alkalosis, low renin and low aldosterone; responds to amiloride or triamterene, not spironolactone

Exam trap: type 2 RTA can show an acidic urine pH, because once serum bicarbonate falls below the lowered proximal threshold, the distal nephron acidifies normally. Do not use urine pH alone to rule it out.

s23c-s110501-1-1.bodyHtml:
The kidneys receive about a fifth of the cardiac output, and the juxtaglomerular apparatus turns any fall in their perfusion into a systemic signal. Renal vascular disease therefore shows up two ways: as hypertension driven by renin, and as ischemic injury to the kidney itself.

Renin release and renovascular hypertension

Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole release renin in response to three inputs: low afferent arteriolar pressure (intrarenal baroreceptor), low sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa, and sympathetic stimulation through beta-1 receptors. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (mostly in pulmonary endothelium) makes angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles (efferent more than afferent at low concentrations), stimulates aldosterone, enhances proximal sodium reabsorption, and stimulates thirst and ADH.

In unilateral renal artery stenosis the poststenotic kidney releases renin; plasma renin and aldosterone are both high (secondary hyperaldosteronism), so hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis can occur. The contralateral kidney, exposed to high pressure, suppresses its own renin and excretes sodium. The stenotic kidney keeps its GFR by angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole; an ACE inhibitor or ARB removes that support, so the GFR of that kidney falls. If both kidneys (or a solitary kidney) depend on it, serum creatinine rises sharply.

Atherosclerotic stenosisFibromuscular dysplasia
WhoOlder adults with vascular risk factors and other atherosclerotic diseaseMainly women aged about 20–60 years
WhereOstium and proximal third of the renal arteryMid and distal renal artery; also carotid and vertebral arteries
PathologyAtheroma with plaque, often bilateralNoninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic; most often medial fibroplasia with alternating thickening and dilation ("string of beads")
KidneyIschemic nephropathy and progressive CKD possibleFunction usually preserved

Hypertensive injury of the kidney

Benign nephrosclerosisMalignant nephrosclerosis
SettingLong-standing hypertension; diabetes and aging also contributeHypertensive emergency (very high pressure with acute organ damage)
Vessel lesionHyaline arteriolosclerosis: glassy pink thickening from plasma proteins leaking into the wallHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (concentric "onion-skin" smooth muscle layers) and fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles
KidneySymmetrically shrunken, finely granular cortical surface; patchy glomerulosclerosis and tubular atrophyPinpoint petechial hemorrhages on the surface ("flea-bitten"); acute kidney injury, hematuria, proteinuria
LabsSlowly falling GFR, modest proteinuriaRising creatinine; often microangiopathic hemolysis; high renin

In people of West African ancestry, two APOL1 risk variants raise the risk of hypertension-attributed CKD and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; much kidney disease once labelled "hypertensive" in this group is APOL1-associated.

Occlusive and embolic disease

  • Renal infarction: usually embolic (atrial fibrillation, left ventricular thrombus, endocarditis) or from dissection or thrombosis. The kidney has end arteries, so the infarct is a pale, wedge-shaped zone of coagulative necrosis with its base on the capsule. Clues: sudden flank or abdominal pain, hematuria, and a very high serum LDH with little or no rise in aminotransferases.
  • Atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal) disease: days to weeks after arterial catheterisation, vascular surgery or anticoagulation, cholesterol crystals from aortic plaque shower small arteries. Biopsy shows biconvex, needle-shaped clefts (crystals dissolved during processing) in arcuate and interlobular arteries with surrounding inflammation. Clues: livedo reticularis, painful blue toes with intact pulses, Hollenhorst plaques in retinal arterioles, eosinophilia, eosinophiluria and low complement. Kidney function often declines stepwise and may not recover.
  • Renal vein thrombosis: most strongly linked to nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy, through urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin), raised hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors V and VIII, platelet activation and hemoconcentration. It can be silent or cause flank pain, hematuria, a rising creatinine and pulmonary emboli. A left renal vein thrombus can cause a new left varicocele, because the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. In newborns, dehydration and maternal diabetes predispose.

Thrombotic microangiopathy and scleroderma renal crisis

Thrombotic microangiopathy (hemolytic uremic syndrome, TTP, malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis, antiphospholipid syndrome, some drugs such as calcineurin inhibitors and gemcitabine) injures endothelium; platelets and fibrin occlude glomerular capillaries and arterioles, and schistocytes appear in blood. In scleroderma renal crisis, intimal proliferation narrows interlobular arteries (an "onion-skin" look), renal perfusion falls and renin rises sharply, giving abrupt hypertension and kidney failure. Risk is highest in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, and after higher-dose glucocorticoids. Because the process is renin driven, ACE inhibitors are the life-saving treatment.

Exam trap: a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected (up to about 30%) and reflects lost efferent tone, not drug toxicity. A much larger rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

Naadi memory aid: "Wedge, needle, beads, onion": wedge infarct from an embolus, needle clefts from cholesterol emboli, a bead string in fibromuscular dysplasia, onion skins in malignant hypertension and scleroderma crisis.

s23c-s110601-1-1.bodyHtml:
Control of micturition

The bladder stores urine at low pressure and empties it completely when the person chooses. Three pathways do this:

PathwayRoots and nerveReceptor and action
ParasympatheticS2–S4, pelvic splanchnic nervesMuscarinic M3 on the detrusor: contraction (voiding)
SympatheticT10–L2, hypogastric nerveBeta-3 on the detrusor: relaxation (storage); alpha-1 at the bladder neck and internal sphincter: closure
SomaticS2–S4, pudendal nerveNicotinic receptors on the external urethral sphincter: voluntary closure

The pontine micturition centre coordinates detrusor contraction with sphincter relaxation, and the frontal cortex decides when voiding is allowed. Where a lesion sits therefore predicts how the bladder behaves.

  • Above the pons (stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, normal pressure hydrocephalus): loss of cortical inhibition gives detrusor overactivity with urgency, but the sphincter still relaxes in step, so residual volume stays low.
  • Spinal cord between the pons and the sacral cord (traumatic injury, multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis): after spinal shock (initial areflexia and retention) the bladder becomes overactive and contracts against a sphincter that closes at the same time, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia. High storage and voiding pressures cause reflux, hydronephrosis, stones, infection and loss of kidney function. With injury at T6 or above, a distended bladder can trigger autonomic dysreflexia (severe hypertension, bradycardia, flushing and headache above the lesion).
  • Sacral cord, cauda equina or peripheral nerves (disc herniation, spina bifida, pelvic surgery, diabetic autonomic neuropathy): the detrusor is underactive, sensation is lost and the bladder overdistends, giving retention with overflow incontinence.

Urinary incontinence: mechanisms

TypeMechanismClue
StressUrethral hypermobility or intrinsic sphincter weakness: pelvic floor (levator ani) and pudendal nerve damage after vaginal birth, obesity, estrogen loss, prostatectomy in menSmall leaks with cough, laugh, lifting; positive cough stress test
UrgeDetrusor overactivity, often idiopathic; also neurologic disease, bladder irritationSudden strong urge, larger leaks, frequency and nocturia
OverflowUnderactive detrusor or outlet obstruction (prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture)Dribbling, weak stream, large post-void residual
FunctionalNormal bladder; patient cannot reach the toilet in time (mobility, cognition)Frail older adult, physical or cognitive limits

Drugs follow the receptors: antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, trospium) block M3 and reduce detrusor contractions; beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron) relax the detrusor through cAMP without anticholinergic effects; alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin) relax the bladder neck and prostate in outlet obstruction. Drugs that cause retention include anticholinergics, opioids, alpha agonists (decongestants) and tricyclic antidepressants.

Urinary tract trauma: anatomy

  • Posterior urethra (prostatic and membranous parts): torn by shearing forces in pelvic fractures, usually at the membranous segment just below the prostate. Blood at the meatus, inability to void, a perineal hematoma and a high-riding or boggy prostate are the signs.
  • Anterior urethra (bulbar and penile parts): the bulbar urethra is crushed against the pubic bone in straddle injuries. If Buck fascia tears, urine and blood spread in the superficial perineal space beneath Colles fascia into the scrotum, penis and lower anterior abdominal wall (deep to Scarpa fascia); attachment of Colles fascia to the fascia lata keeps the fluid out of the thighs.
  • Bladder: extraperitoneal rupture (most common) accompanies pelvic fractures; urine collects around the bladder in the space of Retzius. Intraperitoneal rupture follows a blow to a full bladder, which tears at the dome, the weakest part covered by peritoneum. Urine in the peritoneal cavity causes ascites, ileus and peritonitis, and its urea and creatinine are reabsorbed across the peritoneum, raising serum levels ("pseudo-renal failure").
  • Kidney: protected by ribs and fat; injured by blunt deceleration or penetrating trauma. Deceleration can tear the intima of the renal artery and cause thrombosis. Children are more vulnerable because their kidneys are relatively larger and less padded.
  • Ureter: rarely injured by blunt trauma; most injuries are iatrogenic during gynecologic, colorectal or vascular surgery (near the uterine artery, the pelvic brim and the ovarian vessels).

Obstructive uropathy

Obstruction anywhere from the calyx to the urethra raises pressure behind it. Early, the kidney's blood flow rises briefly and then falls as afferent arterioles constrict; GFR drops. Sustained obstruction dilates the pelvis and calyces (hydronephrosis), compresses the papillae and medulla first, and then thins the cortex through tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a single kidney causes acute kidney injury that is often reversible if relieved early.

  • Causes by age: posterior urethral valves and ureteropelvic junction obstruction in infants; stones in young adults; prostatic enlargement, prostate and bladder cancer, pelvic tumours and retroperitoneal fibrosis in older adults; the gravid uterus (mild right-sided dilation is normal in pregnancy).
  • Posterior urethral valves: obstructing membranous folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of boys, the commonest cause of lower tract obstruction in male infants. The fetus voids poorly, so amniotic fluid falls (oligohydramnios, with pulmonary hypoplasia if severe). Ultrasound shows a thick-walled bladder, a dilated posterior urethra ("keyhole" shape) and bilateral hydronephrosis; voiding cystourethrography confirms it.
  • Post-obstructive diuresis: after relief of bilateral or solitary-kidney obstruction, large volumes of urine can follow. Causes are appropriate excretion of retained urea, salt and water, plus impaired concentrating ability from medullary washout and reduced aquaporin-2 and sodium transporter expression. Watch for hypovolemia, hyponatremia or hypernatremia, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia.

Exam trap: a high serum creatinine after blunt abdominal trauma with a distended abdomen and little urine output is not necessarily kidney injury; intraperitoneal bladder rupture lets the peritoneum reabsorb urine.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Pee is Parasympathetic, Storage is Sympathetic": S2–S4 empties, T10–L2 stores.

s23c-s110701-1-1.bodyHtml:
Three kidneys in sequence

  • Pronephros (week 4, cervical region): never functions in humans and regresses.
  • Mesonephros (weeks 4–8, thoracolumbar): an interim kidney in the first trimester. Its duct, the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, persists in males as the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct, and it gives rise to the ureteric bud in both sexes.
  • Metanephros (from week 5, sacral region): the permanent kidney. Fetal urine production begins around weeks 10–12 and, from the second trimester on, is the main source of amniotic fluid.

Reciprocal induction

The ureteric bud grows out of the distal mesonephric duct into the metanephric mesenchyme (blastema). Each tissue instructs the other: the mesenchyme secretes glial cell–derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), which acts on the RET receptor of the bud to drive its outgrowth and branching, and the branching bud tips induce the mesenchyme to condense and form nephrons.

OriginAdult structures
Ureteric budUreter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, collecting ducts
Metanephric mesenchymeGlomerular (Bowman) capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule
Urogenital sinus (from the cloaca)Bladder (most of it), urethra; the allantois connects the bladder dome to the umbilicus as the urachus, later the median umbilical ligament

When induction fails, the kidney does not form (agenesis) or forms abnormally (dysplasia). The ureteropelvic junction is the last part of the ureter to canalise, which helps explain why it is the commonest site of congenital obstruction.

Ascent

The kidneys start in the pelvis and ascend to the lumbar region between weeks 6 and 9, rotating so the hilum faces medially and taking new arterial branches from the aorta as they rise (which is why accessory renal arteries are common). Failed ascent leaves a pelvic kidney. If the lower poles fuse, the isthmus of the resulting horseshoe kidney is caught under the inferior mesenteric artery. Horseshoe kidney is usually asymptomatic but predisposes to ureteropelvic junction obstruction, stones, infection and, rarely, Wilms tumour; it is associated with Turner syndrome and trisomy 18.

s23c-s110801-1-1.bodyHtml:
The kidney receives about a fifth of the cardiac output, concentrates drugs in its tubules and depends on finely balanced arteriolar tone, so it is one of the commonest targets of drug toxicity. The quickest way to organise nephrotoxins is by where in the nephron they act.

1. Glomerular hemodynamics (prerenal pattern)

Glomerular filtration pressure is set by the balance of afferent and efferent arteriolar tone. When renal perfusion falls (volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis, renal artery stenosis), two compensations keep GFR up: prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole.

  • NSAIDs (including selective COX-2 inhibitors) remove prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation. In a well-hydrated young person this barely matters; in someone whose GFR depends on prostaglandins it causes acute kidney injury. NSAIDs also cause sodium retention, hyperkalemia (low renin and aldosterone), acute interstitial nephritis, minimal change disease (sometimes together with interstitial nephritis), and, with long-term heavy use of combination analgesics, papillary necrosis and chronic interstitial nephritis.
  • ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove angiotensin II tone on the efferent arteriole, so glomerular capillary pressure and GFR fall. A small creatinine rise after starting them is expected and reflects lower intraglomerular pressure, which is the same effect that protects the kidney long term. A large rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis to a single kidney) or volume depletion. They also raise potassium by lowering aldosterone.
  • Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) constrict the afferent arteriole (endothelin, thromboxane, less nitric oxide). Acute toxicity is dose-related and reversible; chronic use gives striped interstitial fibrosis and arteriolar hyalinosis. They also cause hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypertension and, rarely, thrombotic microangiopathy.

Exam trap: the "triple whammy" is an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a diuretic and an NSAID together: volume loss, no efferent constriction and no afferent dilation. Expect a prerenal picture (BUN:creatinine above 20, urine sodium low) in an older patient.

2. Proximal tubule cell injury

Proximal tubule cells reabsorb most filtered solute and take up drugs from both the lumen and the blood, which makes them the main site of direct toxic injury.

DrugHow it injuresPattern
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin)Cationic drug binds megalin on the brush border, is taken up by endocytosis and accumulates in lysosomes until they ruptureNonoliguric acute tubular necrosis after 5–10 days; muddy brown granular casts; magnesium and potassium wasting. Risk rises with trough levels, duration, volume depletion, older age and other nephrotoxins; once-daily dosing lowers risk. Also ototoxic (worse with loop diuretics)
CisplatinTaken up by basolateral organic cation transporters; DNA damage and oxidative injuryAcute tubular necrosis and persistent magnesium wasting; prevented with vigorous isotonic hydration (amifostine is a cytoprotectant option)
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarateTaken up by basolateral organic anion transporters; mitochondrial toxicityProximal tubulopathy: Fanconi syndrome (normoglycemic glycosuria, phosphaturia with hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia, aminoaciduria, proximal RTA). Tenofovir alafenamide gives much lower plasma tenofovir and less kidney toxicity
IfosfamideMetabolite chloroacetaldehydeFanconi syndrome, especially in children; also hemorrhagic cystitis
Iodinated contrastRenal vasoconstriction, medullary hypoxia and direct tubular toxicityCreatinine rise within 24–72 hours, usually transient. The main risk is an eGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73 m², especially with diabetes or volume depletion. Prevent with isotonic IV fluids in high-risk patients and the lowest needed dose; N-acetylcysteine has no proven benefit

3. Tubular lumen: crystals

Drugs that are poorly soluble in urine precipitate in the distal tubule and collecting duct when urine flow is low or the dose is high, causing obstruction and inflammation. Examples are high-dose IV acyclovir (needle-shaped birefringent crystals), methotrexate (precipitates in acidic urine; prevent with hydration and urine alkalinisation, rescue with leucovorin and, in severe toxicity, glucarpidase), sulfadiazine and other sulfonamides, and indinavir (stones and crystals). Prevention is hydration and slower infusion.

4. Distal nephron and collecting duct

  • Amphotericin B binds cholesterol in tubular cell membranes as well as fungal ergosterol and forms pores. In the collecting duct, H+ leaks back and K+ and Mg2+ leak out: distal (type 1) RTA with a urine pH above 5.5, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. It also constricts afferent arterioles. Lipid formulations and saline loading reduce toxicity.
  • Lithium enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), accumulates and inhibits signalling (glycogen synthase kinase-3) that maintains aquaporin-2 expression, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Amiloride blocks ENaC and so reduces lithium entry. Years of use can cause chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with microcysts and CKD; lithium also causes hypercalcemia through hyperparathyroidism.
  • Trimethoprim (and the potassium-sparing diuretics amiloride and triamterene) blocks ENaC, causing hyperkalemia. Trimethoprim and cimetidine also block tubular secretion of creatinine, which raises serum creatinine without any fall in true GFR.

5. Interstitium: acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)

A delayed (type IV, T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity reaction to a drug acting as a hapten. Classic causes are beta-lactams (methicillin historically, nafcillin, penicillins, cephalosporins), proton pump inhibitors, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, rifampin, allopurinol and immune checkpoint inhibitors. It begins days to weeks after exposure (sooner on re-exposure). Fever, rash and eosinophilia occur together in only a minority. Urine shows sterile pyuria, white blood cell casts and mild proteinuria; biopsy shows interstitial edema with lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils, and tubulitis, with normal glomeruli. Stop the drug; corticosteroids are often given when the kidney does not recover promptly.

6. Glomerular disease and other sites

  • Heroin use is linked to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (nephrotic syndrome); NSAIDs to minimal change disease; gold, penicillamine and NSAIDs to membranous nephropathy.
  • Gadolinium-based contrast in patients with advanced CKD or on dialysis can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis: thickening and hardening of skin and connective tissue of the limbs and trunk with joint contractures. Risk is highest with older linear agents; newer macrocyclic agents carry very low risk. It is a toxicity of the skin and connective tissue, not of the kidney itself.
  • Cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide are metabolised to acrolein, which is excreted in urine and injures bladder urothelium: hemorrhagic cystitis (and, long term, bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide). Mesna is a thiol that binds acrolein in the urine; hydration and frequent voiding help.
  • Drug-induced urinary retention: anticholinergics (antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, tricyclic antidepressants, antimuscarinics for overactive bladder) reduce detrusor contraction; alpha-1 agonists (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine) tighten the bladder neck; opioids reduce bladder sensation and detrusor tone. Men with prostatic enlargement are most at risk.

Memory aid (Naadi): walk the drug down the nephron. Arterioles (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors) → proximal cells (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, tenofovir) → lumen (crystals) → collecting duct (amphotericin, lithium) → interstitium (allergic AIN) → bladder (acrolein).

s23c-s150101-1-1.bodyHtml:
Insulin is made in pancreatic beta cells as preproinsulin; cleavage in the endoplasmic reticulum gives proinsulin, and cleavage in secretory granules gives insulin plus C-peptide in equal amounts. C-peptide is not cleared by the liver on first pass and has a longer half-life, so it is the better marker of the patient's own insulin secretion. Injected insulin contains no C-peptide.

How glucose triggers secretion

  1. Glucose enters through GLUT2, a high-capacity transporter that keeps intracellular glucose close to plasma glucose.
  2. Glucokinase (high Km, not inhibited by its product) phosphorylates it, so it acts as the beta cell's glucose sensor.
  3. Glycolysis and oxidation raise the ATP/ADP ratio, which closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels (Kir6.2 pore with the SUR1 subunit).
  4. The membrane depolarises, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, and Ca2+ drives granule exocytosis.
  5. Incretins (GLP-1 and GIP from the gut after a meal) act on Gs-coupled receptors and amplify secretion only when glucose is raised. This is why an oral glucose load releases more insulin than the same glucose given intravenously.

What insulin and glucagon do

ProcessInsulin (fed state)Glucagon (fasting state)
Glucose uptakeMoves GLUT4 to the membrane in skeletal muscle and adipose tissueNo direct effect on muscle
Liver glucose outputSuppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; stimulates glycogen synthesisStimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (cAMP, protein kinase A)
FatStimulates lipogenesis; inhibits hormone-sensitive lipaseLipolysis; with low insulin, fatty acids go to ketogenesis in the liver
ProteinAnabolicPromotes amino acid use for gluconeogenesis
PotassiumDrives K+ into cells (Na+/K+-ATPase)—

The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase; its metabolic effects run mainly through the PI3K-Akt pathway. Brain, red blood cells, kidney medulla and hepatocytes take up glucose without insulin (non-GLUT4 transporters).

Types of diabetes

FeatureType 1Type 2
MechanismT-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of beta cellsInsulin resistance plus progressive relative beta-cell failure
GeneticsHLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 (DQ2/DQ8) association; weaker family concordanceStrongly polygenic; very high concordance in identical twins
Islet histologyInsulitis (lymphocytes in islets), then loss of beta cellsIslet amyloid (amylin, also called islet amyloid polypeptide)
MarkersAutoantibodies to GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 and insulin; low C-peptideNo autoantibodies; C-peptide normal or high early
Typical startChildhood or young adulthood, often with DKAAdulthood with obesity; increasingly in adolescents
Acute crisisDiabetic ketoacidosisHyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (DKA can occur too)
  • Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA): adult-onset autoimmune diabetes, autoantibody positive, that does not need insulin at first but progresses to insulin dependence over months to years.
  • Monogenic diabetes (MODY): autosomal dominant, young onset, not obese, antibody negative. GCK loss raises the glucose set point and gives lifelong mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia with few complications; it usually needs no treatment. HNF1A variants give progressive diabetes with low renal glucose threshold (glycosuria) and marked sensitivity to sulfonylureas.
  • Secondary diabetes: pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, hemochromatosis, pancreatectomy), endocrine excess (Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, glucagonoma, pheochromocytoma) and drugs (glucocorticoids, thiazides, second-generation antipsychotics, calcineurin inhibitors, some HIV protease inhibitors, niacin).

Exam trap: islet amyloid points to type 2, insulitis to type 1. Hemosiderin in islets with bronze skin is hemochromatosis, a secondary cause.

Acute crises: why ketones in one and not the other

FeatureDiabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
InsulinAbsent or nearly soSome insulin remains: enough to restrain lipolysis and ketogenesis, not enough to control glucose
GlucoseRaised, often 250–600 mg/dL; can be near normal with SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycemic DKA)Very high, often above 600 mg/dL
Acid-baseAnion gap metabolic acidosis from beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetateLittle or no acidosis
Osmolality and mental statusMildly raisedMarkedly raised; confusion to coma tracks osmolality
CourseHours to a dayDays of osmotic diuresis and dehydration, often in older adults

Glucagon, cortisol and catecholamines rise in both. Without insulin, hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids that the liver turns into ketoacids. Insulin deficiency also shifts potassium out of cells, so serum K+ may be normal or high while total-body K+ is depleted by urinary losses. Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation; acetone gives a fruity breath odour. Cerebral edema is the feared complication of treatment, especially in children.

Chronic complications

  • Nonenzymatic glycation: glucose attaches to proteins without an enzyme (hemoglobin A1c is the measurable example). Advanced glycation end-products cross-link collagen and basement membranes, trap LDL and plasma proteins and activate inflammatory receptors. Result: thickened capillary basement membranes, hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles, accelerated atherosclerosis.
  • Polyol (sorbitol) pathway: in tissues that take up glucose without insulin (lens, Schwann cells, retina, kidney papillae), aldose reductase reduces excess glucose to sorbitol, which these cells convert slowly. Sorbitol draws in water and depletes NADPH, causing cataracts and peripheral neuropathy.
  • Diabetic kidney disease: early glomerular hyperfiltration, then mesangial expansion, diffuse and then nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson) glomerulosclerosis with PAS-positive nodules, GBM thickening and albuminuria.
  • Retinopathy: pericyte loss, microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages and hard exudates (nonproliferative), then VEGF-driven neovascularisation (proliferative).
  • Neuropathy: distal symmetric "stocking-glove" sensory loss, autonomic neuropathy (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction), mononeuropathies (cranial nerve III palsy that spares the pupil).

Drugs by mechanism

ClassMechanismMain adverse effects
Insulins: rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine), short (regular), intermediate (NPH), long (glargine, detemir, degludec)Replace insulin; differ only in absorption profileHypoglycemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy at injection sites, hypokalemia
Metformin (biguanide)Lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis (in part through AMP-activated protein kinase); improves insulin sensitivityGI upset, vitamin B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis in kidney failure or hypoperfusion; no hypoglycemia alone; weight neutral
Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide); meglitinides (repaglinide)Bind SUR1 and close K-ATP channels, so insulin is released regardless of glucoseHypoglycemia (worst with glyburide, in older adults and in kidney failure), weight gain
Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone)PPAR-gamma agonists (nuclear receptor): raise insulin sensitivity in fat, muscle, liverFluid retention and heart failure, weight gain, fractures
GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide); tirzepatide (GIP and GLP-1 agonist)Glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying, satietyNausea and vomiting, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis; avoid with personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin)Block breakdown of endogenous GLP-1 and GIPGenerally mild; weight neutral; pancreatitis rarely
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin)Block sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, causing glycosuriaGenital mycotic infections, volume depletion, euglycemic DKA; rare necrotising fasciitis of the perineum
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose)Slow carbohydrate digestion at the brush borderFlatulence, diarrhea; treat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose
PramlintideAmylin analogue: slows gastric emptying, lowers glucagonHypoglycemia with insulin (mealtime insulin is reduced), nausea

Memory aid (Naadi): "Closing the door raises the voltage": anything that closes the beta-cell K-ATP door (ATP, sulfonylureas) depolarises the cell and releases insulin; diazoxide props the door open.

s23c-s150102-1-1.bodyHtml:
Hypoglycemia is a plasma glucose low enough to cause symptoms or harm. In a person without diabetes it is investigated only when Whipple's triad is present: symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia, a low plasma glucose measured at the time (in practice below 55 mg/dL, 3.0 mmol/L), and relief of symptoms when glucose is raised. In diabetes care, glucose below 70 mg/dL is level 1, below 54 mg/dL is level 2, and any episode with altered thinking that needs another person's help is level 3 (severe).

The defence against a falling glucose

As glucose falls, the body responds in a fixed order. First, insulin secretion stops. Next, glucagon rises (alpha cells), stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; this is the main fast defence. Epinephrine follows, raising hepatic glucose output, limiting peripheral uptake and producing the warning symptoms. Cortisol and growth hormone act over hours. The brain depends on a steady glucose supply, so prolonged neuroglycopenia causes confusion, seizures, coma and permanent injury.

  • Autonomic (adrenergic and cholinergic) symptoms: tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, tingling.
  • Neuroglycopenic symptoms: confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, focal deficits, seizures, coma.

Reading insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin

Beta cells make proinsulin, which prohormone convertases cleave in secretory granules into insulin and C-peptide in equal molar amounts. Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide. So, during hypoglycemia:

  • High insulin with low C-peptide means injected insulin.
  • High insulin with high C-peptide and proinsulin means the patient's own beta cells are secreting: an insulinoma or a drug that forces secretion (sulfonylurea or meglitinide). Only a drug screen separates these.
  • Beta-hydroxybutyrate is low whenever insulin (or an insulin-like factor) is acting, because insulin blocks lipolysis and ketogenesis. A high ketone level points away from insulin-mediated causes.

Causes

MechanismExamplesClue
DrugsInsulin, sulfonylureas (especially long-acting ones such as glyburide, worse with kidney failure), meglitinides; less often quinine, pentamidine, fluoroquinolonesThe commonest cause overall
EthanolBinge drinking after a period of poor food intakeEthanol oxidation raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio, diverting pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, so gluconeogenesis stalls once glycogen is gone
Hormone deficiencyAdrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism (cortisol and growth hormone loss)Hypoglycemia with hyponatremia, hypotension; children with hypopituitarism
Critical illnessSepsis, liver failure, kidney failure, starvationLess gluconeogenesis, less insulin clearance
Non-islet cell tumour hypoglycemiaLarge mesenchymal tumours (for example a solitary fibrous tumour) or hepatocellular carcinomaTumour secretes incompletely processed ("big") IGF-2, which activates insulin receptors; insulin, C-peptide and ketones are all low
Endogenous hyperinsulinismInsulinoma; post-bariatric hypoglycemia; insulin autoimmune hypoglycemiaSee below

Insulinoma

An insulinoma is a beta-cell neuroendocrine tumour that secretes insulin without regard to glucose. Most are small, solitary and benign and can lie anywhere in the pancreas; multiple tumours suggest MEN1. Hypoglycemia typically occurs during fasting or exercise, and patients often gain weight from eating to prevent symptoms. Because the tumour also releases incompletely processed hormone, the proinsulin fraction is high.

Other forms of endogenous hyperinsulinism

  • Post-bariatric hypoglycemia: after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, food reaches the small bowel quickly, glucose and GLP-1 surge, and insulin overshoots. Symptoms come 1–3 hours after meals, not during fasting.
  • Insulin autoimmune hypoglycemia: antibodies to insulin bind it after meals and release it hours later. Insulin levels are extremely high. It has been linked to sulfhydryl-containing drugs such as methimazole and is more often reported in East Asian populations.
  • Neonatal hypoglycemia in an infant of a mother with diabetes: maternal glucose crosses the placenta, fetal beta cells become hyperplastic, and when the cord is clamped the infant's high insulin output persists while the glucose supply stops.

Other islet cell tumours

Tumour (cell)Hormone actionPicture
Glucagonoma (alpha)Glucagon drives glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and amino acid catabolismNecrolytic migratory erythema (red, crusting, spreading rash, often groin and buttocks), diabetes, weight loss, glossitis, deep venous thrombosis, low amino acids
Somatostatinoma (delta)Somatostatin inhibits insulin, gastrin, cholecystokinin, pancreatic enzymesDiabetes, gallstones, steatorrhea, achlorhydria
VIPoma (non-beta islet cell)Vasoactive intestinal peptide raises cAMP in intestinal epithelium, driving chloride and water secretionLarge-volume watery diarrhea that persists with fasting, hypokalemia, low or absent gastric acid (WDHA)
Gastrinoma (G cells, pancreas or duodenum)Gastrin drives acid secretion and parietal cell growthMultiple or distal ulcers, diarrhea; covered with MEN1

Exam trap: high insulin with high C-peptide does not prove an insulinoma. A sulfonylurea gives the same pattern, so a drug screen comes before any pancreatic imaging.

Memory aid (Naadi): "The needle leaves no peptide": injected insulin brings no C-peptide with it.
