s23c-s150201-1-1.bodyHtml:
The thyroid makes thyroxine (T4) and, in smaller amounts, the active hormone triiodothyronine (T3). Almost every Step 1 thyroid question rests on four ideas: where the gland comes from, how iodide becomes hormone, how the axis is regulated, and where drugs act.

Development

  • The thyroid begins as an endodermal outgrowth at the foramen cecum, at the junction of the anterior two thirds and posterior third of the tongue. It descends in front of the hyoid and larynx, attached by the thyroglossal duct, which normally disappears.
  • Thyroglossal duct cyst: a midline neck mass, usually at or just below the hyoid, that rises when the tongue is protruded or with swallowing. Surgical excision removes the central part of the hyoid with the tract to prevent recurrence. A lateral neck mass at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid is a branchial cleft cyst instead.
  • Lingual thyroid: failure of descent leaves thyroid tissue at the tongue base; it may be the only thyroid tissue the patient has, so it is imaged before any removal.
  • Parafollicular C cells (calcitonin) come from the ultimobranchial body of the fourth pharyngeal pouch, with neural crest contribution.

Hormone synthesis

  1. Trapping: the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) on the basolateral membrane concentrates iodide. Perchlorate and pertechnetate compete for it.
  2. Oxidation and organification: at the apical membrane, thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, forming monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT).
  3. Coupling: TPO joins DIT + DIT to make T4, and MIT + DIT to make T3.
  4. Release: TSH drives endocytosis of colloid; lysosomal proteases free T4 and T3. Large iodide doses and lithium inhibit release.

The gland secretes mostly T4. Peripheral 5′-deiodinase (types 1 and 2) converts T4 to T3, the form that binds nuclear receptors; type 3 deiodinase makes inactive reverse T3. Over 99% of circulating hormone is protein-bound, mostly to thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), and only the free fraction acts.

TBG changeCausesTotal T4Free T4 and TSH
IncreasedPregnancy, estrogen (oral contraceptives, hormone therapy), acute hepatitis, tamoxifenHighNormal
DecreasedAndrogens, glucocorticoids, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosisLowNormal

Regulation

Hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary TSH, which acts through a Gs-coupled receptor (cAMP) to drive every step of synthesis and to cause follicular hypertrophy. T3 inside thyrotrophs and the hypothalamus feeds back negatively. Because TSH responds steeply to small changes in free T4, TSH is the most sensitive screening test in primary thyroid disease, but it is unreliable when the pituitary itself is diseased.

Actions of thyroid hormone

  • Raises basal metabolic rate through more Na+/K+-ATPase activity and heat production.
  • Increases cardiac β1-receptor expression: tachycardia, raised contractility and cardiac output.
  • Essential for brain maturation and bone growth in infancy (untreated congenital deficiency causes permanent intellectual disability).
  • Increases glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; lowers LDL by raising hepatic LDL receptors.

Pharmacology by mechanism

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects
MethimazoleBlocks TPO (organification and coupling)Agranulocytosis (rare, early), rash, cholestatic hepatitis; first-trimester embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal or esophageal atresia)
Propylthiouracil (PTU)Blocks TPO and peripheral 5′-deiodinaseAgranulocytosis; severe hepatocellular injury (boxed warning); ANCA-associated vasculitis
Levothyroxine (T4)Replacement; converted to T3 in tissuesOver-replacement: atrial fibrillation, bone loss
Propranolol and other β-blockersControl adrenergic symptoms; propranolol at high dose slightly reduces T4 to T3 conversionBronchospasm, bradycardia
Radioactive iodine (131I)Taken up by NIS; β-emission destroys follicular cellsPermanent hypothyroidism (expected); can worsen active Graves orbitopathy; contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Potassium iodide (iodine solution)Large doses acutely block organification (Wolff-Chaikoff) and hormone releaseGiven only after a thionamide in hyperthyroidism, or it fuels new hormone synthesis

Drugs that disturb thyroid function: amiodarone (about a third iodine by weight) can cause hypothyroidism (failure to escape Wolff-Chaikoff, especially with underlying Hashimoto) or thyrotoxicosis (type 1: iodine-driven synthesis in a nodular or Graves gland; type 2: destructive thyroiditis); lithium blocks hormone release and causes goiter and hypothyroidism; immune checkpoint inhibitors cause thyroiditis.

Exam trap: a woman on oral contraceptives with a high total T4 and a normal TSH is euthyroid. The extra hormone is bound to the extra TBG; free T4 is normal.

Memory aid (Naadi): "PTU works Peripherally Too": it is the thionamide that also blocks T4-to-T3 conversion.

s23c-s150201-1-2.bodyHtml:
Hypothyroidism: Hashimoto thyroiditis

Chronic autoimmune (lymphocytic) thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate. It is much more common in women and associated with HLA-DR3 and DR5 and with other autoimmune diseases. Anti-TPO (and anti-thyroglobulin) antibodies are present; destruction is mostly cell-mediated (cytotoxic T cells, apoptosis). Early follicular destruction may release stored hormone and cause brief thyrotoxicosis ("hashitoxicosis").

  • Gross: diffusely enlarged, firm, painless goiter; late in the disease the gland may shrink.
  • Microscopy: dense lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centres; atrophic follicles; Hürthle (oncocytic) cells, large follicular cells with granular pink cytoplasm full of mitochondria.
  • Risk: primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell or MALT type), which presents as a rapidly enlarging thyroid in a patient with long-standing Hashimoto.

Other causes of hypothyroidism: iodine deficiency (endemic goiter, worldwide the leading cause), prior radioiodine or thyroidectomy, drugs (amiodarone, lithium, checkpoint inhibitors), central (pituitary or hypothalamic) disease, and congenital dysgenesis. Clinical effects of deficiency include cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes, dry skin, menorrhagia, hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia, raised creatine kinase and nonpitting myxedema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation.

Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease

  • Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (IgG against the TSH receptor) mimics TSH: diffuse hyperplasia, a smooth goiter with a bruit, high radioiodine uptake, suppressed TSH. It is a type II (antibody-mediated, receptor-stimulating) hypersensitivity. The antibody crosses the placenta and can cause transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis.
  • Microscopy: tall, crowded follicular cells with papillary infoldings; pale colloid with "scalloped" edges where it is being resorbed.
  • Orbitopathy: orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes express TSH receptors (and IGF-1 receptors). Autoantibodies and T-cell cytokines drive fibroblasts to secrete hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronan) and to become fat cells, expanding extraocular muscles and orbital fat: proptosis, lid retraction, diplopia, and in severe cases optic nerve compression. Smoking and radioiodine worsen it.
  • Dermopathy: pretibial myxedema, the same glycosaminoglycan deposition in the shin dermis.

Other causes of thyrotoxicosis: toxic multinodular goiter and toxic adenoma (autonomous nodules, often activating TSH-receptor mutations, no orbitopathy), thyroiditis (leakage of stored hormone, low uptake), exogenous hormone, iodine load (Jod-Basedow), hCG-mediated (hyperemesis, molar pregnancy), struma ovarii and, rarely, a TSH-secreting adenoma.

Thyroiditis compared

TypeSetting and cluesPathologyCourse
Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain)After a viral upper respiratory illness; painful, tender gland, fever, very high ESRGranulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells around damaged folliclesThyrotoxic, then hypothyroid, then usually normal over months; low radioiodine uptake while thyrotoxic
Painless (silent) and postpartumPainless; postpartum form within a year of delivery; anti-TPO often positiveLymphocytic infiltrate without the germinal centres and fibrosis of HashimotoSame three-phase course; recurs after later pregnancies; some develop permanent hypothyroidism
HashimotoPainless goiter, hypothyroidismLymphoid follicles, Hürthle cellsPermanent hypothyroidism common
Riedel (fibrous)Rock-hard, fixed gland that can compress the trachea; mimics cancerDense fibrosis extending beyond the capsule; IgG4-positive plasma cells (part of IgG4-related disease)Variable; may need steroids or surgery

Nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick syndrome)

Severe illness, starvation and high-dose glucocorticoids reduce 5′-deiodinase activity, so T3 falls and reverse T3 rises; with longer, more severe illness T4 and TSH can also fall. Thyroid hormone is not given; values recover as the illness resolves, sometimes with a transient TSH overshoot.

Thyroid neoplasms

TumourCell and geneticsHistologyBehaviour
Follicular adenomaFollicular cellEncapsulated, no capsular or vascular invasionBenign; FNA cannot tell it from carcinoma
Papillary carcinoma (about 80–85%)Follicular cell; BRAF V600E, RET/PTC rearrangements; childhood radiation exposurePapillae; nuclei with clear "ground glass" chromatin, grooves and pseudoinclusions; psammoma bodiesSpreads to cervical lymph nodes; excellent prognosis
Follicular carcinomaFollicular cell; RAS mutations, PAX8-PPARGDiagnosis needs capsular or vascular invasionHematogenous spread (bone, lung)
Medullary carcinomaParafollicular C cell; RET (sporadic or MEN2)Nests of cells in amyloid stroma derived from calcitonin (Congo red)Calcitonin and CEA are tumour markers; does not take up iodine
Anaplastic carcinomaFollicular cell, dedifferentiated; TP53Pleomorphic, spindle and giant cellsOlder adults; rapidly growing, invasive; very poor prognosis
Primary lymphomaB cell; arises in HashimotoSheets of lymphoid cellsRapidly enlarging gland; treated with chemotherapy and radiation

Exam trap: a painful thyroid with thyrotoxicosis and low radioiodine uptake is subacute thyroiditis, not Graves. Thionamides do nothing, because no new hormone is being made.

s23c-s150301-1-1.bodyHtml:
Serum calcium is held in a narrow range by three hormones acting on three organs: bone, kidney and gut. About 40% of total calcium is bound to albumin, so a low albumin lowers total calcium without changing the ionised fraction. A common bedside correction adds 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL; measuring ionised calcium is more reliable. Alkalosis increases albumin binding and lowers ionised calcium, which is why hyperventilation causes perioral tingling.

The three hormones

HormoneSource and triggerMain actions
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)Chief cells; secreted when ionised calcium falls, sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR, a G protein-coupled receptor)Bone: stimulates osteoblasts to express RANKL, which activates osteoclasts and releases calcium and phosphate. Kidney: raises calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule (phosphaturia), stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)Skin (cholecalciferol) → liver 25-hydroxylation → proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylation, driven by PTH and low phosphate, inhibited by FGF23Raises intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate; needed for normal mineralisation; feeds back to suppress PTH.
CalcitoninParafollicular C cells of the thyroid, released by high calciumInhibits osteoclasts; minor physiologic role in adults; tumour marker for medullary thyroid cancer.

FGF23 from osteocytes lowers phosphate by blocking proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption and suppressing 1-alpha-hydroxylase; it rises early in chronic kidney disease. Magnesium is needed both for PTH release and for target-organ response, so severe hypomagnesemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism that does not correct until magnesium is replaced.

Hypercalcemia

Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy cause about 90% of cases. The first test after confirming true hypercalcemia is an intact PTH.

  • PTH high or inappropriately normal (PTH-dependent): primary hyperparathyroidism (single adenoma in about 85%, four-gland hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma), familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), lithium, tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
  • PTH suppressed (PTH-independent): PTH-related peptide (PTHrP) from squamous cell, renal, bladder, breast and ovarian cancers; osteolytic metastases or multiple myeloma; calcitriol made by granulomas (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) or lymphoma macrophages; vitamin D or A excess; thiazides; milk-alkali syndrome; immobilisation; thyrotoxicosis.

Symptoms reflect calcium level and speed of rise: kidney stones, polyuria from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, bone pain and osteitis fibrosa cystica (subperiosteal resorption of the radial side of the middle phalanges, "salt-and-pepper" skull, brown tumours), constipation, peptic ulcer and pancreatitis, fatigue, depression and confusion, and a short QT interval.

FHH is usually caused by a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in CASR (autosomal dominant). The parathyroids and kidney "read" calcium as low, so PTH is normal or mildly high and the kidney avidly reabsorbs calcium: urine calcium is low, with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio usually below 0.01. It is benign and parathyroidectomy does not help. A homozygous loss of CaSR in a newborn causes severe neonatal hyperparathyroidism.

Exam trap: mild hypercalcemia with a normal-to-high PTH is not always primary hyperparathyroidism. Check urine calcium; a very low calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio and a family history of the same labs point to FHH.

content.text: Serum calcium is held in a narrow range by three hormones acting on three organs: bone, kidney and gut. About 40% of total calcium is bound to albumin, so a low albumin lowers total calcium without changing the ionised fraction. A common bedside correction adds 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL; measuring ionised calcium is more reliable. Alkalosis increases albumin binding and lowers ionised calcium, which is why hyperventilation causes perioral tingling.
Chief cells; secreted when ionised calcium falls, sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR, a G protein-coupled receptor)

Bone: stimulates osteoblasts to express RANKL, which activates osteoclasts and releases calcium and phosphate. Kidney: raises calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule (phosphaturia), stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
Skin (cholecalciferol) → liver 25-hydroxylation → proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylation, driven by PTH and low phosphate, inhibited by FGF23
Raises intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate; needed for normal mineralisation; feeds back to suppress PTH.

Inhibits osteoclasts; minor physiologic role in adults; tumour marker for medullary thyroid cancer.

FGF23 from osteocytes lowers phosphate by blocking proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption and suppressing 1-alpha-hydroxylase; it rises early in chronic kidney disease. Hypocalcemia

Low ionised calcium raises neuromuscular excitability: perioral and fingertip paresthesia, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign with a blood pressure cuff), facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve (Chvostek sign), laryngospasm, seizures and a prolonged QT interval.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A results from a loss-of-function variant in GNAS, which encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit (Gs-alpha) that couples the PTH receptor to adenylyl cyclase. In the kidney and some other tissues only the maternal allele is expressed (imprinting), so the variant inherited from the mother gives PTH resistance plus Albright hereditary osteodystrophy: short stature, round face, obesity, shortened fourth and fifth metacarpals and subcutaneous ossification. s23c-s150401-1-1.bodyHtml:
The adrenal gland is two organs in one capsule. The cortex (mesoderm) makes steroids from cholesterol; the medulla (neural crest) is a modified sympathetic ganglion that makes catecholamines.

LayerMain productMain regulator
Zona glomerulosaAldosteroneAngiotensin II and serum potassium (ACTH only minor)
Zona fasciculataCortisolACTH
Zona reticularisAndrogen precursors (DHEA, DHEA sulfate)ACTH
MedullaEpinephrine (mostly), norepinephrinePreganglionic sympathetic (acetylcholine, nicotinic receptors); cortisol from the cortex induces PNMT, which makes epinephrine

Adrenal insufficiency

  • Primary (Addison disease): the gland itself fails. In high-income countries autoimmune adrenalitis is most common (antibodies to 21-hydroxylase, often with other autoimmune endocrine disease); worldwide, tuberculosis. Other causes: bilateral hemorrhage (anticoagulation, antiphospholipid syndrome, meningococcal sepsis as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), metastases (lung, breast), fungal infection, adrenoleukodystrophy in boys and young men.
  • Both cortisol and aldosterone are lost. Low aldosterone gives hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, mild metabolic acidosis and salt craving with volume depletion. Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so the pituitary makes more pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC); its cleavage products ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone darken skin creases, scars and the buccal mucosa.
  • Secondary (pituitary) and tertiary (hypothalamic, including after stopping long-term glucocorticoids): ACTH is low, so there is no hyperpigmentation, and because renin-angiotensin still drives the glomerulosa, aldosterone is preserved and hyperkalemia is absent. Hyponatremia can still occur, because cortisol deficiency raises ADH release.

Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess)

Features: central obesity with thin limbs, facial rounding, dorsocervical fat, wide purple striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infections, mood change; in children, weight gain with slowing linear growth.

CauseACTHClue
Exogenous glucocorticoid (most common overall)LowIncludes inhaled, topical or injected steroids, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir; the adrenals are atrophic
Pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease; most common endogenous cause)Normal or highUsually a microadenoma; cortisol suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone; bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
Ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer, bronchial and other carcinoids)Often very highRapid onset, hypokalemia and alkalosis (cortisol overwhelms renal 11β-HSD2), hyperpigmentation; no suppression with high-dose dexamethasone
Adrenal adenoma or carcinomaSuppressedContralateral adrenal atrophic; carcinoma is large and often also makes androgens

Mineralocorticoid excess

Primary aldosteronism (bilateral zona glomerulosa hyperplasia or an aldosterone-producing adenoma) is the commonest curable cause of hypertension. Aldosterone raises ENaC activity in principal cells, so sodium is retained and potassium and hydrogen ions are lost: hypertension, low renin, metabolic alkalosis and, in a minority, hypokalemia. Edema is absent because of "aldosterone escape" (pressure natriuresis and natriuretic peptides).

ConditionReninAldosteroneMechanism
Primary aldosteronismLowHighAutonomous aldosterone
Renovascular hypertension, renin-secreting tumour, diureticsHighHighSecondary aldosteronism
Liddle syndromeLowLowGain-of-function ENaC (autosomal dominant); treated with amiloride or triamterene
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess, heavy licorice intakeLowLow11β-HSD2 deficient or inhibited, so cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor
11β-hydroxylase or 17α-hydroxylase deficiencyLowLowExcess 11-deoxycorticosterone acts as a mineralocorticoid

Adrenal medulla and tumours

  • Pheochromocytoma: a catecholamine-secreting chromaffin-cell tumour (a paraganglioma if outside the adrenal). Paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension (sustained or episodic), pallor, anxiety, hyperglycemia. Chromogranin-positive nests of cells ("zellballen") with sustentacular cells. Roughly a third or more carry a germline variant: RET (MEN2), VHL, NF1, succinate dehydrogenase genes (paragangliomas, higher malignancy risk), so genetic testing is offered to everyone.
  • Neuroblastoma: the most common extracranial solid tumour of early childhood, arising from neural crest cells of the medulla or sympathetic chain. A firm, irregular abdominal mass that may cross the midline, with periorbital bruising from orbital metastases, Horner syndrome, opsoclonus-myoclonus (paraneoplastic) or hypertension. Small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes; urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid raised. MYCN amplification predicts aggressive disease.
  • Adrenocortical carcinoma: rare, usually large (often over 6 cm) and heterogeneous, frequently secreting cortisol and androgens together (rapid Cushing syndrome with virilisation); associated with Li-Fraumeni (TP53) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes.
NeuroblastomaWilms tumour
AgeMost under 5 years (median under 2)Usually 2–5 years
MassIrregular, may cross the midline, calcified on imagingSmooth, rarely crosses the midline
MarkersRaised urine HVA and VMANone; hematuria in some
GeneticsMYCN amplification (poor prognosis)WT1, WT2 region

Exam trap: hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation both point to a primary adrenal problem. A patient with adrenal insufficiency and a normal potassium and no pigmentation more likely has pituitary disease or glucocorticoid withdrawal.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Salt, Sugar, Sex" from the outside in: glomerulosa keeps salt, fasciculata raises sugar, reticularis makes sex steroid precursors.

s23c-s150501-1-1.bodyHtml:
Development and anatomy

The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) grows up from the roof of the primitive mouth as Rathke pouch (surface ectoderm). The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) grows down from the floor of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm) and is really a bundle of hypothalamic axon terminals. The anterior lobe has no direct arterial supply of note: it receives hypothalamic releasing hormones through the low-pressure hypophyseal portal veins of the stalk, which is why it is vulnerable to ischemia and why stalk damage changes its output. The gland sits in the sella turcica under the optic chiasm, with the cavernous sinuses (cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, and the internal carotid artery) on each side.

Hormones and signalling

HormoneCellReceptor signallingMain control
GHSomatotroph (acidophil)Cytokine-type receptor, JAK2-STATGHRH up; somatostatin and IGF-1 down; sleep, exercise, hypoglycemia raise it; hyperglycemia lowers it
ProlactinLactotroph (acidophil)Cytokine-type receptor, JAK2-STATTonic inhibition by dopamine (D2) from the arcuate nucleus; TRH and estrogen raise it
ACTHCorticotroph (basophil), cut from POMCMC2R, cAMPCRH and ADH up; cortisol down
TSH, LH, FSHBasophils; share an alpha subunit with hCGGs, cAMPTRH; pulsatile GnRH; sex steroids and inhibin feed back
ADH (vasopressin)Hypothalamic neurons, released from posterior lobeV2 (Gs, cAMP, aquaporin-2) in collecting duct; V1 (Gq) on vesselsPlasma osmolality (main), volume and pressure, nausea, pain
OxytocinHypothalamic neurons, posterior lobeGqSuckling, cervical stretch

Pituitary adenomas

Most are benign monoclonal tumours. Microadenomas are under 1 cm; macroadenomas are 1 cm or more and cause mass effects:

  • Bitemporal hemianopia from pressure on the crossing nasal retinal fibres in the chiasm.
  • Hypopituitarism, typically losing GH and gonadotropins first, then TSH, then ACTH.
  • Stalk effect: compression of the stalk stops dopamine reaching the lactotrophs, so prolactin rises modestly (usually below about 100 ng/mL) even though the tumour does not make prolactin.
  • Lateral spread into the cavernous sinus causes diplopia from cranial nerve palsies.

Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning adenoma. Prolactin suppresses GnRH, giving amenorrhea, infertility and galactorrhea in women, and low libido, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men (who present later, often with macroadenomas). Dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) act on D2 receptors to cut secretion and shrink the tumour.

Somatotroph adenoma causes gigantism if it starts before the epiphyses close and acromegaly after: coarse features, frontal bossing, prognathism, widened tooth gaps, large hands and feet, carpal tunnel syndrome, sweating, sleep apnea, insulin resistance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy, arthropathy and colonic polyps. Many tumours carry activating GNAS mutations (constitutive Gs signalling); McCune-Albright syndrome is the mosaic form. Treatment options by mechanism: somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide) reduce GH release; pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so IGF-1 falls while GH rises (monitor IGF-1, not GH).

Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch remnants. It is the commonest supratentorial tumour of childhood that affects the pituitary, with a second peak in older adults. It is suprasellar, cystic and often calcified, filled with dark, oily fluid. The adamantinomatous (childhood) type has beta-catenin (CTNNB1) mutations and wet keratin; the papillary (adult) type carries BRAF V600E. It causes headache, bitemporal field loss, growth failure, diabetes insipidus and, after surgery, hypothalamic obesity.

Ischemia: Sheehan syndrome and apoplexy

In pregnancy the anterior lobe nearly doubles in size (lactotroph hyperplasia) but its portal blood supply does not. Severe postpartum hemorrhage with hypotension can then cause ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). The first sign is often failure to lactate, followed by no return of menses, fatigue, hypotension and hyponatremia from cortisol and thyroid deficiency. Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma: thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and acute adrenal insufficiency.

Water balance

Central diabetes insipidus (now also called AVP deficiency) is lack of ADH; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (AVP resistance) is a collecting duct that cannot respond (V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 variants, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia). Both give large volumes of dilute urine. SIADH is the opposite: ADH secreted despite low plasma osmolality, so free water is retained. The patient is clinically euvolemic because volume expansion triggers natriuresis (natriuretic peptides up, renin-aldosterone down), so urine sodium is high. Causes include small cell lung cancer (ectopic ADH), CNS disease, lung disease, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine), pain, nausea and postoperative states.

Exam trap: a modestly raised prolactin with a large sellar mass is not necessarily a prolactinoma. Prolactinomas big enough to compress the chiasm usually raise prolactin far higher. Think stalk effect from a nonfunctioning adenoma, and remember the opposite pitfall, the hook effect: with a giant prolactinoma, very high prolactin can saturate the assay and read falsely low unless the sample is diluted.

Memory aid (Naadi): the pituitary loses its jobs in the order "Grow, Get pregnant, Thyroid, Then stress": GH, gonadotropins, TSH, then ACTH.

s23c-s1506-1-1.bodyHtml:
The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems. It makes the releasing and inhibiting hormones that reach the anterior pituitary through the portal veins, makes ADH and oxytocin for the posterior pituitary, and controls appetite, temperature, thirst and circadian rhythm.

Nuclei worth knowing

RegionMain roleDamage causes
Supraoptic and paraventricular nucleiADH (mainly supraoptic) and oxytocin (mainly paraventricular); paraventricular also makes CRH and TRHCentral diabetes insipidus
Arcuate nucleusDopamine (prolactin inhibition), GnRH, GHRH; senses leptin and insulinHyperprolactinemia, hypogonadism, appetite dysregulation
Ventromedial nucleusSatietyHyperphagia and obesity
Lateral hypothalamic areaHunger, arousal (orexin neurons)Anorexia and weight loss; loss of orexin neurons causes narcolepsy with cataplexy
Anterior hypothalamus (preoptic)Heat loss (sweating, vasodilation); sets the febrile set point under prostaglandin E2Hyperthermia
Posterior hypothalamusHeat conservation (shivering, vasoconstriction)Poikilothermia (body temperature drifts with the environment)
Suprachiasmatic nucleusCircadian clock, driven by light through the retinohypothalamic tract; controls pineal melatoninDisrupted sleep-wake rhythm

Appetite signalling

Leptin from fat cells and insulin act on the arcuate nucleus. They stimulate POMC neurons, which release alpha-MSH onto MC4 receptors in the paraventricular nucleus to signal satiety, and they inhibit neuropeptide Y/AgRP neurons, which drive hunger. Ghrelin from the stomach does the opposite. Loss-of-function variants in MC4R are the commonest single-gene cause of severe early-onset obesity; congenital leptin deficiency (treated with leptin) is rare. In ordinary obesity leptin is high, reflecting leptin resistance.

GnRH and reproduction

GnRH must be released in pulses. Pulsatile GnRH stimulates LH and FSH; continuous GnRH (or a long-acting GnRH agonist) desensitises gonadotrophs and suppresses them, which is the basis of agonist therapy for precocious puberty and prostate cancer.

  • Kallmann syndrome: GnRH neurons start in the olfactory placode and migrate along olfactory axons into the forebrain. Variants such as ANOS1 (X-linked) or FGFR1 disrupt this migration, giving hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia or hyposmia (low GnRH, low LH and FSH, low sex steroids). Other features: cleft lip or palate, renal agenesis, mirror movements. The same deficiency with a normal sense of smell is normosmic idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
  • Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: energy deficit (restricted eating, heavy exercise) and psychological stress slow GnRH pulses through low leptin, high cortisol and other signals. LH and FSH are low or normal and estradiol is low, so there is no withdrawal bleed after progestin. Long-term risk: loss of bone density and stress fractures.
  • Hypothalamic hamartoma: a benign malformation containing GnRH-producing neurons (and glial cells that stimulate GnRH release) that drives central precocious puberty, sometimes with gelastic (laughing) seizures.
  • Opioids, high-dose glucocorticoids, hyperprolactinemia and critical illness all suppress GnRH.

Structural and infiltrative disease

Masses (craniopharyngioma, germinoma, glioma), radiation, trauma and infiltration damage the hypothalamus. Langerhans cell histiocytosis (CD1a- and langerin-positive cells with Birbeck granules, often with BRAF V600E) and sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas) classically thicken the stalk and cause central diabetes insipidus, often with anterior pituitary deficiencies. Damage to the osmoreceptors can cause adipsic diabetes insipidus: no thirst, so hypernatremia is severe. Prader-Willi syndrome (loss of paternally expressed genes at 15q11-q13) shows hypothalamic dysfunction: infant hypotonia and poor feeding, then hyperphagia, obesity, short stature and hypogonadism.

Exam trap: hypogonadism with low LH and FSH is a hypothalamic or pituitary problem; with high LH and FSH it is a gonadal problem. Ask about smell before ordering anything else.

s23c-s1507-1-1.bodyHtml:
The multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are autosomal dominant conditions in which tumours arise in several endocrine glands, often in young adults, often in more than one gland, and often bilaterally. Two different genetic mechanisms explain the two main families.

MEN1: loss of a tumour suppressor

The MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13 encodes menin, a nuclear protein that restrains cell proliferation through effects on transcription and chromatin. Affected people inherit one inactive copy; a tumour forms when the second copy is lost in a cell (the two-hit model), which is why tumours are multiple and appear in several glands over time.

  • Parathyroid: hyperplasia of all four glands, the commonest and usually the earliest feature, presenting with hypercalcemia, stones or bone loss at a younger age than sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Pancreas and duodenum: neuroendocrine tumours. Gastrinomas in MEN1 are usually small, multiple and in the duodenal wall; insulinomas and nonfunctioning tumours also occur. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are a leading cause of death in MEN1.
  • Anterior pituitary: adenomas, most often prolactinomas.
  • Others: foregut carcinoid tumours (thymic, bronchial, gastric), adrenal cortical nodules, facial angiofibromas and collagenomas, lipomas.

Hypercalcemia stimulates gastrin release, so uncontrolled hyperparathyroidism makes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome in MEN1 worse.

MEN2: gain of function of a receptor tyrosine kinase

The RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10q11) encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed in neural crest derivatives. In MEN2, a single activating (gain-of-function) mutation makes the receptor signal without its ligand. The neural crest cells involved are the thyroid parafollicular C cells and the adrenal medullary chromaffin cells.

MEN2AMEN2B
Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)Nearly all carriers, preceded by C-cell hyperplasiaNearly all, earlier (childhood) and more aggressive
PheochromocytomaAbout half, often bilateralAbout half
Primary hyperparathyroidismA minority (hyperplasia)Absent
OtherCutaneous lichen amyloidosis (itchy plaques over the upper back); Hirschsprung disease in some familiesMucosal neuromas of lips, tongue and eyelids; intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (constipation, megacolon); marfanoid habitus without lens or aortic disease
Typical RET variantCysteine codons in the extracellular domain (634 is the classic high-risk codon)M918T in the kinase domain

Medullary thyroid carcinoma

MTC arises from C cells, which secrete calcitonin; the tumour also releases CEA, and both serve as tumour markers. Microscopically, nests of polygonal or spindle cells sit in a stroma of amyloid derived from calcitonin, which stains with Congo red. Serum calcium is usually normal despite high calcitonin. Because C cells neither concentrate iodine nor depend on TSH, radioactive iodine and TSH suppression have no role. About a quarter of MTC is hereditary, which is why every patient with MTC is offered germline RET testing.

Hirschsprung disease and RET

Loss-of-function RET variants impair migration of neural crest cells to the distal bowel and cause Hirschsprung disease. Some MEN2A families carry variants that both activate the receptor in C cells and reduce its signalling at the cell surface in enteric neurons, so the two conditions can occur together.

Exam trap: MEN1 is a loss-of-function tumour suppressor (two hits); MEN2 is a gain-of-function proto-oncogene (one hit). Hyperparathyroidism belongs to MEN1 and MEN2A, never MEN2B.

Memory aid (Naadi): "MEN1 counts the glands from the neck down to the belly and up to the head": parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary. MEN2 is the neural crest pair: C cells and chromaffin cells.

Normal sex development

Until about week 7 the gonads are bipotential and both duct systems are present. On the Y chromosome, SRY starts testis development; without it an ovary forms.

Testis cellProductEffect
Sertoli cellAnti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)Regression of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts, so no uterus, fallopian tubes or upper vagina
Leydig cellTestosteroneWolffian (mesonephric) ducts become epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles
Target tissuesDihydrotestosterone (DHT), made by 5α-reductase type 2Penis, scrotum, prostate; male external genitalia

Without AMH the Müllerian ducts persist; without testosterone the Wolffian ducts regress; without DHT the external genitalia look female or ambiguous. Androgens, not ovaries, are needed to virilise, which is why androgen exposure masculinises a 46,XX fetus.

Differences (disorders) of sex development

The term covers congenital conditions in which chromosomal, gonadal or anatomic sex develops atypically. Use neutral, respectful language with families.

ConditionKaryotypeInternalExternal genitaliaKey labs

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

An autosomal recessive defect in cortisol synthesis. Low cortisol raises ACTH, which enlarges both adrenals and pushes precursors into whichever pathways remain open (see the figure).

EnzymeMineralocorticoid effectAndrogensTypical picture
21-hydroxylase (about 95% of cases)Aldosterone low: salt wasting, hypotension, hyperkalemia (classic salt-wasting form)HighVirilised 46,XX newborn; adrenal crisis at 1–3 weeks, often unrecognised in boys; nonclassic form presents later with hirsutism or early pubarche
11β-hydroxylase11-deoxycorticosterone high: hypertension, hypokalemiaHighVirilisation with hypertension
17α-hydroxylase11-deoxycorticosterone high: hypertension, hypokalemiaLowUndervirilised 46,XY or absent puberty in 46,XX, with hypertension

Congenital hypothyroidism

  • Worldwide the leading cause is maternal iodine deficiency. Where iodine intake is adequate, most cases are thyroid dysgenesis: an absent, small or ectopic gland (often at the tongue base, from failed descent along the thyroglossal duct from the foramen cecum). The rest are defects in hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis, for example thyroid peroxidase variants, often with goiter); a few are central or transient (maternal blocking antibodies, iodine exposure).
  • Maternal T4 crosses the placenta, so most newborns look normal at birth. Untreated infants develop prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, constipation, hypotonia, a large tongue, umbilical hernia, a large posterior fontanelle and dry skin, followed by irreversible intellectual disability and growth failure. Newborn screening exists to prevent this.

Kallmann syndrome

Failure of GnRH neurons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during development: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (delayed puberty, low LH, FSH and sex steroids) with anosmia or hyposmia.

Exam trap: a uterus is present in any 46,XX condition and absent in any 46,XY condition with working Sertoli cells (androgen insensitivity, 5α-reductase deficiency), because AMH depends on the testis, not on androgen action.

Memory aid (Naadi): in CAH the enzyme number tells the blood pressure: 21 drops it (salt lost), 11 and 17 lift it (deoxycorticosterone builds up).

s23c-s150901-1-1.bodyHtml:
Many drugs change endocrine function by acting on a hormone's feedback loop, its synthesis, its receptor or the assay that measures it. Thinking in those four steps makes most questions predictable.

Exogenous glucocorticoids

Supraphysiologic glucocorticoids (roughly more than 5 mg/day of prednisone or equivalent) suppress CRH and ACTH by negative feedback. Without ACTH the zona fasciculata and reticularis atrophy, so cortisol and adrenal androgens fall. The zona glomerulosa is controlled mainly by angiotensin II and potassium, so aldosterone is preserved. Suppression is likely after about 3 weeks of a supraphysiologic dose, and recovery can take months.

Effects of glucocorticoid excess by mechanism: gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance (hyperglycemia), protein catabolism (proximal myopathy, thin skin, striae, poor wound healing), reduced osteoblast function and gut calcium absorption (osteoporosis, osteonecrosis of the femoral head), central fat redistribution, immunosuppression with lymphopenia and neutrophil demargination (a raised neutrophil count), eosinopenia, cataracts, glaucoma, mood change and growth suppression in children.

Drugs acting on the adrenal and steroid pathways

DrugActionEndocrine consequence
EtomidateInhibits 11-beta-hydroxylaseTransient cortisol suppression after a single induction dose
KetoconazoleInhibits several cytochrome P450 steroidogenic enzymesLowers cortisol and testosterone; gynecomastia; used for Cushing syndrome
MetyraponeInhibits 11-beta-hydroxylaseLowers cortisol; 11-deoxycortisol rises
MitotaneAdrenolytic to the cortexAdrenal insufficiency; used for adrenocortical carcinoma
SpironolactoneMineralocorticoid and androgen receptor antagonistHyperkalemia, gynecomastia
FludrocortisoneMineralocorticoid agonistReplaces aldosterone; excess causes hypertension and hypokalemia
Opioids (long-term)Suppress hypothalamic GnRH and CRHHypogonadotropic hypogonadism; occasionally central adrenal insufficiency

Anabolic-androgenic steroids

Exogenous testosterone and its analogues suppress GnRH, LH and FSH. Low LH means low intratesticular testosterone, so the testes shrink and spermatogenesis stops (infertility). Other effects: erythrocytosis, low HDL and high LDL, acne, gynecomastia (aromatisation to estradiol), hepatotoxicity and hepatic adenoma with oral 17-alpha-alkylated agents, mood change and, in adolescents, premature epiphyseal closure. After stopping, hypogonadism can persist for months.

The thyroid and iodine-rich drugs

  • Amiodarone is about one third iodine by weight and inhibits type 1 deiodinase (less T4 to T3 conversion, higher reverse T3).
    • Hypothyroidism: the iodine load triggers the Wolff-Chaikoff effect (iodine excess inhibits organification); glands with underlying autoimmune thyroiditis fail to escape it.
    • Type 1 thyrotoxicosis: iodine fuels excess hormone synthesis in a gland with nodules or latent Graves disease (Jod-Basedow phenomenon).
    • Type 2 thyrotoxicosis: a destructive thyroiditis from direct drug toxicity, releasing stored hormone.
  • Iodinated contrast can cause Jod-Basedow thyrotoxicosis in an older patient with multinodular goiter.
  • Lithium is concentrated by the thyroid and inhibits hormone release, causing goiter and hypothyroidism. It also raises the calcium set point of the CaSR, giving hypercalcemia with high PTH, and causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
  • Drugs that raise thyroxine-binding globulin (oral estrogen, tamoxifen) raise total T4 with normal free T4; in a patient on levothyroxine, estrogen increases the dose needed. Drugs that impair levothyroxine absorption include calcium, iron, proton pump inhibitors and bile acid sequestrants.

Glucose

Drugs that raise glucose: glucocorticoids, thiazides (hypokalemia reduces insulin release), atypical antipsychotics (weight gain, insulin resistance; olanzapine and clozapine most), protease inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus is toxic to beta cells), statins (small rise in diabetes incidence), niacin and nonselective beta-blockers (which can also mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia). SGLT2 inhibitors cause glucosuria, lower insulin needs and raise glucagon, so ketogenesis can proceed with near-normal glucose: euglycemic DKA, triggered by surgery, fasting, illness or reduced insulin dose.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors

Releasing T-cell brakes can cause autoimmune endocrine disease. Anti-CTLA-4 agents (ipilimumab) most often cause hypophysitis (headache, central adrenal insufficiency, central hypothyroidism, hypogonadism). Anti-PD-1/PD-L1 agents (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) most often cause thyroiditis (transient thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism) and, rarely, abrupt insulin-deficient diabetes. Unlike most immune adverse events, endocrinopathies are usually permanent and are managed with hormone replacement rather than high-dose glucocorticoids.

Prolactin

Dopamine from the tuberoinfundibular pathway tonically inhibits prolactin. D2 antagonists (risperidone and first-generation antipsychotics, metoclopramide) and dopamine-depleting drugs raise prolactin, causing galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, low libido and, over time, low bone density.

Exam trap: secondary adrenal insufficiency from stopping glucocorticoids spares aldosterone, so potassium is usually normal. Hyperkalemia points to primary adrenal failure.

Memory aid (Naadi): "CTLA-4 hits the head, PD-1 hits the neck": hypophysitis with ipilimumab, thyroiditis with nivolumab and pembrolizumab.

s23c-s110101-2-1.bodyHtml:
Classify first

Management depends on where the infection is and who has it.

  • Acute uncomplicated cystitis: a healthy, nonpregnant, premenopausal or postmenopausal woman with dysuria, frequency and urgency, and no fever, flank pain or systemic signs.
  • Complicated UTI: infection beyond the bladder (fever, flank pain, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or infection in a patient with features that predict failure: pregnancy, male sex, catheter, obstruction or stones, urologic abnormality, kidney transplant or significant immunocompromise.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: bacteria in a properly collected urine without symptoms of UTI.

Uncomplicated cystitis

A typical history is enough; a dipstick helps when the story is unclear. Urine culture is not needed for a first, typical episode, but is obtained for recurrence, failure, atypical symptoms or any complicated feature. First-line choices:

DrugUsual courseAvoid or limit when
Nitrofurantoin5 dayseGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73 m², suspected pyelonephritis (inadequate tissue levels)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole3 daysLocal resistance above about 20%, use in the past 3 months, sulfa allergy
FosfomycinSingle doseSlightly less effective; not for pyelonephritis
Pivmecillinam3–5 daysPenicillin allergy

Fluoroquinolones and beta-lactams are second line for cystitis: they work, but fluoroquinolones carry tendon, aortic, neurologic and C. difficile risks, and short beta-lactam courses fail more often.

Pyelonephritis

  • Obtain a urinalysis and a urine culture before antibiotics in every case; blood cultures if septic or admitted.
  • Outpatient (stable, able to take oral fluids): an oral fluoroquinolone for 5–7 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 7–14 days when the isolate is susceptible. Where fluoroquinolone resistance is common, give one initial parenteral dose of a long-acting agent such as ceftriaxone.
  • Admit for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, suspected obstruction or failure of oral therapy; start an IV agent such as ceftriaxone, broadened (for example to piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) when there is septic shock or risk of resistant organisms.
  • Imaging (CT abdomen and pelvis, or ultrasound when contrast or radiation should be avoided) is for severe illness, suspected stone or obstruction, or no improvement after 48–72 hours. It finds abscess, obstruction and emphysematous pyelonephritis.
  • Infected obstructed kidney is a urologic emergency: antibiotics alone fail, so decompress urgently with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Stone removal waits until the infection clears.
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in the renal parenchyma, nearly always in diabetes): IV antibiotics with percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy if that fails.

Special populations

  • Pregnancy: screen once with a urine culture early in pregnancy (around 12–16 weeks) and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, because untreated bacteriuria leads to pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Safe choices include cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin (avoid nitrofurantoin near term and, if alternatives exist, in the first trimester; avoid trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the first trimester and near term; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines). Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is treated in hospital with IV beta-lactam therapy, and many clinicians then give suppressive therapy for the rest of the pregnancy.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria outside pregnancy is not screened for or treated, including in older adults, people with diabetes, spinal cord injury or long-term catheters. The other exception is a planned urologic procedure that breaches the mucosa (for example transurethral resection of the prostate).
  • Men: every UTI is treated as complicated; treat for about 7 days, longer (up to 14 days) if prostatitis is suspected or response is slow.
  • Catheter-associated UTI: diagnose only with symptoms (fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium without another cause). Remove the catheter if possible, or replace a catheter that has been in place for more than about 2 weeks, and send culture from the new catheter before antibiotics.
  • Recurrent UTI (2 or more in 6 months or 3 or more in a year): confirm each episode with culture. Options are behavioural measures, vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women, post-coital or continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis, and patient-started treatment. Image the tract only if there are atypical features (for example, recurrence with Proteus, hematuria between infections, or a man).

Exam trap: a confused nursing-home resident with a positive urine culture and no urinary symptoms or fever does not have a UTI. Look for another cause and do not treat the bacteriuria.

s23c-s110102-2-1.bodyHtml:
Recognise glomerular bleeding

Hematuria is glomerular when red cells are dysmorphic (acanthocytes), when there are red cell casts, or when it comes with proteinuria, hypertension or a rising creatinine. Glomerular hematuria needs a nephrology work-up rather than cystoscopy first. A patient whose creatinine is rising over days to weeks with an active sediment has rapidly progressive GN until proven otherwise, which is a medical emergency.

First tests

  • Urinalysis with microscopy; spot urine protein-to-creatinine (or albumin-to-creatinine) ratio; serum creatinine and electrolytes.
  • Serology chosen by the picture: C3 and C4; ANA and anti-dsDNA; ANCA (MPO and PR3 by immunoassay); anti-GBM antibody; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B; hepatitis B and C, HIV; cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor; serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains in older adults.
  • Kidney biopsy is the most accurate test and also grades activity and chronicity. In suspected rapidly progressive GN, start treatment without waiting for biopsy when serology is positive and the patient is deteriorating.

Treatment by disease

DiseaseManagement
Post-streptococcal GNSupportive: sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretic for edema and hypertension, other antihypertensives as needed; antibiotics only for persisting streptococcal infection. Immunosuppression is not used. Persistently low C3 after about 8 weeks suggests another diagnosis (for example C3 glomerulopathy or lupus).
IgA nephropathySupportive care is the base: ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to the highest tolerated dose, blood pressure control, an SGLT2 inhibitor when eGFR allows, and lifestyle measures; aim to lower proteinuria well below 1 g/day. Patients with persistent proteinuria at high risk of progression are considered for glucocorticoid-based or newer targeted therapies.
Anti-GBM diseasePlasma exchange to remove the antibody, plus glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, started urgently. Patients who need dialysis at presentation and have crescents in nearly all glomeruli rarely recover kidney function unless they have lung hemorrhage that needs treatment anyway.
ANCA-associated GNInduction with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; the C5a receptor blocker avacopan can reduce glucocorticoid exposure; plasma exchange may be added for very severe kidney failure or anti-GBM overlap. Maintenance with rituximab (or azathioprine). Screen for and prevent Pneumocystis infection.
Lupus nephritis III or IV (± V)Glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide, with add-on belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor (voclosporin) in many patients; hydroxychloroquine for every patient with lupus unless contraindicated; ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria. Mycophenolate is teratogenic: use effective contraception and switch to azathioprine before a planned pregnancy.
Cryoglobulinemic GN (hepatitis C)Direct-acting antivirals; rituximab, with plasma exchange for severe disease.

Indications for kidney biopsy in lupus

Biopsy a patient with lupus who has proteinuria of about 0.5 g/day or more, an active sediment (dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts) or an unexplained rise in creatinine. The class decides treatment, so it is not skipped.

Exam trap: a smoker with hemoptysis and kidney failure may have anti-GBM disease or ANCA vasculitis, and some patients have both antibodies. Send both serologies, and do not delay plasma exchange and immunosuppression while waiting for biopsy if the patient is deteriorating.

s23c-s110102-2-2.bodyHtml:
Confirm and characterise

  • Quantify proteinuria with a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (about 3–3.5 g/g or more is nephrotic range); 24-hour collection is rarely needed.
  • Check albumin, lipids, creatinine, glucose and hemoglobin A1c, and the secondary-cause panel: hepatitis B and C, HIV, ANA, complement, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains, and anti-PLA2R antibody.
  • Children aged about 1 to 10 years with typical nephrotic syndrome (normal complement, no gross hematuria, normal kidney function and blood pressure) are presumed to have minimal change disease and given oral glucocorticoids without biopsy; biopsy is for steroid resistance or atypical features.
  • Adults usually need a biopsy. An exception: a typical adult with nephrotic syndrome, preserved function and a positive anti-PLA2R antibody can be diagnosed with primary membranous nephropathy without biopsy.

General measures for any nephrotic patient

  • Dietary sodium restriction and a loop diuretic for edema (higher doses are often needed because the diuretic is protein bound in urine and less albumin carries it to the kidney).
  • ACE inhibitor or ARB to lower intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, with blood pressure control.
  • Statin for persistent hyperlipidemia when the disease is not expected to remit soon.
  • Prophylactic anticoagulation is considered when albumin is very low (for example below about 2.0–2.5 g/dL), especially with membranous nephropathy and low bleeding risk; established venous thrombosis is treated with full anticoagulation.
  • Pneumococcal and seasonal influenza vaccination.

Disease-specific treatment

DiseaseTreatment
Minimal changeGlucocorticoids (most remit within weeks); for frequent relapses or steroid dependence, steroid-sparing agents such as rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors or cyclophosphamide. Stop an offending NSAID; look for lymphoma in an adult with suggestive features.
Primary FSGSSupportive care plus high-dose glucocorticoids; calcineurin inhibitor if resistant. Secondary FSGS is treated by addressing the cause (antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated nephropathy, weight loss, stopping heroin or lithium) with RAS blockade; immunosuppression does not help secondary or genetic forms.
MembranousSupportive care for low-risk disease, since about a third remit spontaneously; rituximab (or cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids, or a calcineurin inhibitor) for moderate to high risk. Anti-PLA2R levels track response. For PLA2R-negative disease in an older adult, look for a secondary cause, including age-appropriate cancer screening.
Diabetic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB, SGLT2 inhibitor, and in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist (finerenone) and a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven kidney benefit (see the CKD section).
AL amyloidosisConfirm with tissue (fat-pad or kidney biopsy with Congo red) and typing; treat the plasma cell clone.

Renal vein thrombosis

Suspect it in a nephrotic patient (classically membranous) with sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, a rise in creatinine, a raised LDH or an unexplained pulmonary embolism. Confirm with CT or MR venography (Doppler ultrasonography is an alternative), and anticoagulate.

Acute interstitial nephritis

Suspect AIN with a rising creatinine after a new drug, especially with pyuria, white cell casts, rash, fever or eosinophilia. The first step is to stop the likely drug. If creatinine does not improve within several days, or the injury is severe, confirm with biopsy and give glucocorticoids. Checkpoint-inhibitor AIN is treated with glucocorticoids and holding the drug.

Exam trap: a 4-year-old with new nephrotic syndrome and normal complement does not need a biopsy first. Start prednisone, and biopsy only if there is no remission.

s23c-s110201-2-1.bodyHtml:
The incidental renal cyst

Cysts found on CT or ultrasound done for another reason are classified by their CT (or MRI) features, using the Bosniak classification, which estimates the chance of malignancy.

ClassFeaturesAction
IThin smooth wall, no septa, calcification or solid parts, water density, no enhancementBenign: no follow-up
IIA few thin septa, fine calcification, or a small uniformly high-density nonenhancing cystBenign: no follow-up
IIFMore numerous or minimally thickened septa or wall; no measurable enhancing noduleImaging surveillance ("F" for follow-up) over several years
IIIThickened, irregular, enhancing walls or septaSurgical excision (often partial nephrectomy) or, for small cysts or frail patients, active surveillance
IVEnhancing soft-tissue nodule within the cystTreat as cancer: partial or radical nephrectomy (surveillance only if surgery is a poor option)

Ultrasound alone can confirm a simple cyst. An indeterminate lesion on ultrasound needs renal-protocol CT or MRI with contrast. Biopsy is rarely needed for cysts.

ADPKD: diagnosis

  • With a family history, ultrasound is the usual test. In families of unknown genotype, the number of cysts that confirms the diagnosis rises with age (for example, at least 3 cysts in total between 15 and 39 years; at least 2 in each kidney between 40 and 59 years). A normal ultrasound after 40 essentially excludes the disease. MRI is more sensitive in younger relatives being considered as kidney donors, and genetic testing settles unclear cases.
  • Total kidney volume (from MRI or CT) predicts the rate of decline and identifies rapid progressors.

ADPKD: management

  • Blood pressure: an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker first line (the RAAS is the driver). In younger patients with preserved GFR, a lower target (around 110/75 mm Hg) slows kidney growth if tolerated.
  • Fluids and salt: generous water intake (to suppress vasopressin) and dietary sodium restriction; avoid nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.
  • Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) for adults at risk of rapidly progressive disease (for example, large total kidney volume for age, or a fast fall in eGFR). It causes polyuria, thirst and nocturia, and it can cause serious liver injury, so liver tests are checked regularly, most closely in the first 18 months.
  • Pain and bleeding: most cyst hemorrhage settles with rest, fluids and analgesia (avoid NSAIDs when GFR is reduced).
  • Cyst infection: fever and focal pain, sometimes with negative urine cultures. Diagnose with imaging (MRI, or PET-CT when unclear) and treat for several weeks with a lipid-soluble antibiotic that enters cysts, such as a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; drain large infected cysts that do not respond.
  • Intracranial aneurysm screening: offer MR angiography to patients with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage, a prior rupture, a high-risk job (for example, pilots) or before major elective surgery. Routine screening of everyone is not recommended.
  • Kidney failure: dialysis or transplant; native nephrectomy if kidneys are so large they leave no room for the graft or cause recurrent bleeding or infection.

Benign solid masses

  • Angiomyolipoma: macroscopic fat on CT is diagnostic. Small asymptomatic tumours are watched with imaging. Treatment (selective arterial embolisation, nephron-sparing surgery or an mTOR inhibitor in tuberous sclerosis) is considered for symptoms, growth, large size or in women planning pregnancy. Acute retroperitoneal hemorrhage with shock is treated with resuscitation and emergency selective arterial embolisation, which stops bleeding while sparing kidney tissue.
  • Oncocytoma: a central scar on imaging is suggestive but not reliable; biopsy can suggest it, but because it can resemble chromophobe carcinoma, most enhancing solid masses are managed as possible cancer.

Exam trap: a sudden severe headache in a young adult with ADPKD is a ruptured berry aneurysm until proved otherwise: noncontrast CT head first.

s23c-s110202-2-1.bodyHtml:
Hematuria: the work-up

  1. Confirm: a positive dipstick also reacts to myoglobin and free hemoglobin, so confirm with urine microscopy. Microscopic hematuria is 3 or more red cells per high-power field on a properly collected specimen.
  2. Look for benign or glomerular causes: infection (treat and repeat), menstruation, vigorous exercise or recent instrumentation (repeat later); dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, proteinuria or a rising creatinine point to glomerular disease and nephrology referral rather than urologic imaging.
  3. Gross hematuria without an obvious benign cause, even once and even on anticoagulants, needs multiphase CT urography and cystoscopy.
  4. Microscopic hematuria is risk-stratified (age, sex, smoking, degree of hematuria, other risk factors). High-risk patients (for example older smokers or more than 25 red cells per high-power field) get CT urography and cystoscopy; low-risk patients (for example a young nonsmoking woman with 3–10 red cells) may be rechecked with a repeat urinalysis or evaluated after shared decision-making with cystoscopy and renal ultrasonography.

The solid renal mass

  • Characterise with renal-protocol CT or MRI (with contrast): enhancement means a solid tumour, fat means angiomyolipoma. Stage with chest imaging.
  • Localised small masses (up to about 4 cm, T1a): partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy is preferred, because preserving kidney function lowers later CKD and cardiovascular risk. Thermal ablation or active surveillance suits older or frail patients; biopsy helps when the result would change management.
  • Larger or central tumours, or renal vein involvement: radical nephrectomy, with thrombectomy for a vena caval thrombus.
  • After nephrectomy for clear cell RCC at high risk of recurrence, adjuvant pembrolizumab is an option.
  • Metastatic clear cell RCC: first-line systemic therapy is an immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination (a PD-1 inhibitor with a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or nivolumab with ipilimumab). Conventional chemotherapy and hormonal therapy do not work.
  • VHL disease: lifelong surveillance (abdominal MRI, eye examination, brain and spine MRI, plasma metanephrines); small renal tumours are watched and removed with nephron-sparing surgery once they reach about 3 cm; belzutifan is an option for VHL tumours that do not need immediate surgery.

Bladder cancer

  • Transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) diagnoses, stages (it must sample detrusor muscle) and treats non-invasive disease.
  • Non-muscle-invasive, low risk: TURBT, often with one immediate post-resection instillation of intravesical chemotherapy, then surveillance cystoscopy.
  • Non-muscle-invasive, high grade or carcinoma in situ: TURBT (repeat resection for T1 tumours) followed by intravesical BCG induction and maintenance. Radical cystectomy if BCG fails.
  • Muscle-invasive (T2 or higher), no metastases: cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy with urinary diversion; bladder-sparing trimodality therapy (maximal TURBT with chemoradiation) is an alternative for selected patients.
  • Upper-tract urothelial carcinoma: CT urography and ureteroscopy with biopsy; usually nephroureterectomy, with endoscopic treatment for small low-grade tumours. Test for Lynch syndrome when appropriate.

Wilms tumour

  • An abdominal mass in a young child: abdominal ultrasonography first (solid versus cystic, kidney versus adrenal, renal vein and caval involvement), then CT or MRI of the abdomen and CT of the chest. Avoid repeated palpation, which can rupture the capsule.
  • Treatment combines nephrectomy and chemotherapy (plus radiation for advanced stages); cure rates are high for favourable histology.
  • Surveillance in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and other high-risk syndromes: abdominal (renal) ultrasonography every 3 months until about age 7; in Beckwith-Wiedemann, alpha-fetoprotein is also checked in early childhood for hepatoblastoma.

Exam trap: hematuria in a patient taking warfarin or a DOAC is still worked up fully; anticoagulation unmasks lesions, it does not explain them.

s23c-s110301-2-1.bodyHtml:
Hematuria: confirm, exclude benign causes, then stratify

  1. Confirm a positive dipstick with microscopy. Microscopic hematuria is 3 or more red cells per high-power field on a properly collected specimen; a dipstick alone is not enough to start an evaluation.
  2. Exclude benign or transient causes: menstruation, vigorous exercise, recent instrumentation, sexual activity and urinary infection. Treat an infection and repeat the urinalysis afterwards.
  3. Look for a glomerular source: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, proteinuria, rising creatinine or new hypertension point to the kidney; refer to nephrology (urologic evaluation may still be needed if risk is high).
  4. Stratify risk of urothelial cancer in nonglomerular hematuria. Risk rises with age, male sex, smoking (pack-years), the number of red cells per field and a history of gross hematuria. Other risk factors: occupational exposure to aromatic amines or benzene dyes, cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation, aristolochic acid, chronic catheter.
Risk group (AUA microhematuria guidance)Typical featuresEvaluation
LowYounger women and men, little or no smoking, 3–10 red cells per field, no other risk factorsShared decision: repeat urinalysis within about 6 months, or cystoscopy with renal ultrasonography
IntermediateMiddle age, moderate smoking, 11–25 red cells per field, or persistent low-risk hematuriaCystoscopy and renal ultrasonography
HighAge 60 years or older, more than 30 pack-years, more than 25 red cells per field, or any gross hematuriaCystoscopy and CT urography (multiphase CT with an excretory phase)

Gross hematuria without an obvious benign cause (for example, a clear infection that resolves) needs cystoscopy and CT urography in adults, even if it happened once. Anticoagulation does not explain hematuria: patients on anticoagulants are evaluated in the same way. If contrast cannot be given, use MR urography or noncontrast imaging with retrograde pyelography.

Proteinuria: quantify and classify

  • A positive dipstick is followed by a quantitative spot ratio (UACR for albuminuria in diabetes and chronic kidney disease, UPCR when overall protein matters). Categories of albuminuria: A1 below 30, A2 30–300 and A3 above 300 mg/g.
  • Repeat a positive test: transient proteinuria from fever, exercise or acute illness disappears.
  • In adolescents and young adults with low-grade proteinuria, normal blood pressure and normal kidney function, check a first-morning sample (or a split collection of upright and recumbent urine). Protein only when upright is orthostatic proteinuria, which is benign and needs reassurance and perhaps a recheck.
  • Persistent proteinuria: serum creatinine and eGFR, urine microscopy, blood pressure, glucose and A1c, and, depending on the context, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains (age over 40, anemia, hypercalcemia), complement, ANA, hepatitis B and C, HIV. Nephrotic-range protein, active sediment or falling eGFR prompt nephrology referral and often biopsy.

Oliguria and acute retention

In any patient with a sudden fall in urine output, first rule out obstruction: bladder scan or straight catheterisation (post-void residual above about 200 mL suggests retention), and flush or replace an existing catheter. Common causes in older men are prostatic enlargement, anticholinergic or opioid drugs and constipation. After relief of prolonged obstruction, watch for a post-obstructive diuresis (urine output above about 200 mL/h) with losses of sodium, potassium and water. Only then pursue prerenal and intrinsic causes (see acute kidney injury).

Red or dark urine with few red cells

  • Rhabdomyolysis: heme-positive dipstick, few red cells, creatine kinase often above about 5 times normal (often far higher), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, early hypocalcemia. Treat with early, generous isotonic fluids aiming at high urine output; stop the offending drug.
  • Intravascular hemolysis: pink plasma, low haptoglobin, high LDH, hemoglobinuria; for example G6PD deficiency after an oxidant drug.

Exam trap: a patient taking warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant who develops hematuria still gets the full evaluation. Anticoagulation unmasks lesions; it rarely causes bleeding from a normal urinary tract.

s23c-s110401-2-1.bodyHtml:
Definition and staging (KDIGO)

AKI is any of: serum creatinine up by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; creatinine at least 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days; or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.

StageCreatinineUrine output
11.5–1.9 × baseline, or rise of at least 0.3 mg/dLBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours
22.0–2.9 × baselineBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
33 × baseline, or creatinine 4.0 mg/dL or more, or start of kidney replacement therapyBelow 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours or more, or anuria for 12 hours or more

First steps in every case

  1. Review the history and medicines: volume losses, hypotension, contrast, nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam), ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics.
  2. Assess volume status at the bedside.
  3. Urinalysis with microscopy (casts, cells, crystals), urine sodium, creatinine and urea for fractional excretion.
  4. Check for obstruction: bladder scan or catheter for retention; renal ultrasound for hydronephrosis.
  5. Check potassium, bicarbonate and calcium/phosphate; review drug doses for the current GFR.

By cause

  • Prerenal from volume loss: isotonic crystalloid; creatinine should improve within 24–72 hours. In heart failure or cirrhosis, "prerenal" means low effective volume; treat the cause (diuresis for congestion, albumin and vasoconstrictors for hepatorenal syndrome).
  • ATN: supportive; keep euvolemia, stop nephrotoxins, adjust doses, avoid hyperkalemia, and wait for recovery over 1–3 weeks.
  • Postrenal: relieve the obstruction (urethral catheter for bladder outlet obstruction; stent or nephrostomy for ureteral obstruction). Watch for post-obstructive diuresis.
  • Rhabdomyolysis: early, generous isotonic fluids aiming for a high urine output; treat hyperkalemia; avoid giving calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcemia, which often rebounds during recovery.
  • Tumor lysis syndrome: prevent in high-risk patients with IV fluids and rasburicase (converts uric acid to soluble allantoin; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency); allopurinol for intermediate risk.
  • Contrast-associated AKI: in people at high risk (low eGFR), give isotonic IV fluid before and after contrast and stop nephrotoxins; do not withhold an indicated contrast study for fear of AKI alone.

When to start dialysis urgently

Dialysis is started for complications that do not respond to medical treatment:

  • severe metabolic acidosis;
  • hyperkalemia not controlled medically;
  • dialysable poisons (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates);
  • volume overload with pulmonary edema despite diuretics;
  • uremic complications: pericarditis, encephalopathy, uremic bleeding.

A creatinine or BUN number alone is not an indication.

Exam trap: a pericardial friction rub in a patient with advanced kidney failure is uremic pericarditis, an indication for urgent dialysis. NSAIDs and colchicine, the usual pericarditis treatments, are not the answer.

Staging (KDIGO): cause, GFR and albuminuria

GFR categoryeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)
G190 or more (with kidney damage)
G260–89 (with kidney damage)
G3a45–59
G3b30–44
G415–29
G5Below 15 (kidney failure)

Albuminuria by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR): A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30–300 mg/g, A3 above 300 mg/g. Risk rises with both lower GFR and higher ACR, so both are reported (for example "G3a A3"). Confirm abnormal ACR on repeat testing. Screen people with diabetes and hypertension yearly with eGFR and ACR.

Slowing progression

  • Blood pressure: KDIGO suggests a systolic target below 120 mm Hg when tolerated, measured in a standardised way.
  • ACE inhibitor or ARB (one, not both) at the highest tolerated dose for albuminuria (especially A3, and A2 with diabetes). Check creatinine and potassium after starting; accept a creatinine rise up to about 30%.
  • SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes with CKD and eGFR at least 20, and for CKD without diabetes when eGFR is at least 20 and ACR is at least 200 mg/g or heart failure is present. Continue it once started, even as eGFR falls, until dialysis.
  • Finerenone (nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist) in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria despite maximal ACE inhibitor or ARB, if eGFR is at least 25 and potassium is normal.
  • GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes with CKD when more is needed beyond metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors.
  • Statin for adults 50 years and older with CKD; stop smoking; avoid NSAIDs; dose-adjust drugs (metformin is reduced at eGFR below 45 and stopped below 30).

Treating complications

ComplicationApproach
AnemiaExclude other causes; replete iron first (ferritin and transferrin saturation; IV iron is often needed). An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) is considered for persistent hemoglobin below 10 g/dL; avoid targeting normal hemoglobin (13 g/dL or more), which raises stroke and thrombosis risk
Mineral and bone disorderLower phosphate (diet, then phosphate binders); correct vitamin D deficiency; for progressive secondary hyperparathyroidism, calcitriol or a calcimimetic (cinacalcet); parathyroidectomy for refractory or tertiary disease
Metabolic acidosisOral sodium bicarbonate when serum bicarbonate is persistently low (below about 18 mEq/L)
HyperkalemiaLow-potassium diet; stop potassium-raising drugs that are not essential; loop or thiazide diuretic; potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to keep RAS blockade going
Volume overload, edemaSodium restriction and loop diuretics

Planning kidney replacement

Refer to nephrology at eGFR below 30 (or earlier for heavy albuminuria or rapid decline). At G4, discuss the options: transplant (best survival; preemptive transplant before dialysis is ideal), hemodialysis (create an arteriovenous fistula months ahead, and protect the non-dominant arm from venipuncture), peritoneal dialysis, or conservative care. Start dialysis for symptoms or complications, not at a fixed eGFR.

Exam trap: do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB; dual blockade raises hyperkalemia and AKI without renal benefit.

s23c-s110401-2-3.bodyHtml:
Presentation

Sudden, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, with nausea and hematuria (gross or microscopic). Pain does not ease with position, unlike peritonitis. Fever with a stone means possible infected obstruction.

Imaging

  • Noncontrast low-dose CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the most accurate test and shows size and location.
  • Ultrasound first in pregnancy and in children, and reasonable in young adults with a typical recurrent episode; it shows hydronephrosis even when it misses small ureteral stones.

Acute management

  • Analgesia: an NSAID (for example ketorolac) is first line when kidney function allows; add opioids if needed.
  • Stones up to 10 mm without complications: trial of passage with hydration and pain control. For distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm, an alpha blocker (tamsulosin) improves passage. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own. Strain the urine and send the stone for analysis.
  • Urgent urology (decompression by stent or nephrostomy) for infection with obstruction, AKI, obstruction of a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, or pain or vomiting that cannot be controlled.
  • Elective removal (ureteroscopy, shock wave lithotripsy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large or staghorn stones) for stones that do not pass in about 4–6 weeks or are too large to pass.

Workup after a stone

Everyone: stone analysis, serum calcium, creatinine, electrolytes and uric acid, and urinalysis. High-risk or recurrent stone formers (children, solitary kidney, multiple or recurrent stones, bowel disease): a 24-hour urine for volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium and creatinine. A high serum calcium leads to PTH testing for primary hyperparathyroidism.

Prevention

FindingPrevention
Low urine volume (all types)Fluids for a urine output of at least 2.5 L/day
HypercalciuriaLow sodium intake, normal dietary calcium (do not restrict), limit animal protein; thiazide if stones recur
HypocitraturiaPotassium citrate
HyperoxaluriaLimit high-oxalate foods; calcium with meals; in enteric hyperoxaluria, low-fat diet and calcium supplements with meals
Uric acid stonesPotassium citrate to raise urine pH to about 6–6.5; allopurinol if hyperuricosuria persists
Calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuriaAllopurinol
CystineVery high fluid intake, alkalinisation, then tiopronin
StruviteComplete stone removal and treatment of infection

Exam trap: a low-calcium diet raises the risk of calcium oxalate stones, because less calcium is left in the gut to bind oxalate.
