s23c-s110501-2-1.bodyHtml:
When to suspect renovascular hypertension

  • Hypertension starting before about 30 years (think fibromuscular dysplasia, especially in women) or a new, severe or resistant hypertension after about 55 years.
  • A rise in serum creatinine of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • Recurrent "flash" pulmonary edema with preserved ejection fraction, or unexplained kidney atrophy or a size difference of more than about 1.5 cm between kidneys.
  • An abdominal or flank bruit, especially one with a diastolic component; diffuse atherosclerosis.
  • Hypokalemia with high renin and high aldosterone (contrast primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin).

Imaging

TestUse
Renal artery duplex ultrasonographyNoninvasive first test in many centres; no contrast; operator dependent, limited by obesity and bowel gas
CT angiographyExcellent detail of the arteries and the beaded pattern of fibromuscular dysplasia; needs iodinated contrast
MR angiographyAlternative when iodinated contrast is undesirable; gadolinium is avoided in severe CKD (eGFR below 30) unless a lower-risk group II agent is used
Catheter angiographyReference standard; done when intervention is planned, with pressure gradients across the lesion

In fibromuscular dysplasia, image the arteries from head to pelvis once (CT angiography), because carotid, vertebral and other lesions and aneurysms are common.

Treatment

  • Atherosclerotic stenosis: medical therapy first: blood pressure control (an ACE inhibitor or ARB is appropriate in unilateral disease, with creatinine and potassium checked within 1–2 weeks), a high-intensity statin, antiplatelet therapy, smoking cessation and diabetes control. Large randomised trials found that adding stenting to optimal medical therapy did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events in typical patients. Revascularisation is considered for recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rapidly declining kidney function attributable to the stenosis, or truly refractory hypertension.
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia with hypertension: percutaneous transluminal angioplasty without a stent, which often improves or cures the hypertension, especially in younger patients with short-duration disease; antiplatelet therapy is commonly given.

Renal infarction

Suspect it in a patient with atrial fibrillation or another embolic source who has acute flank pain, hematuria and a high LDH, especially when a stone is not seen. Contrast-enhanced CT (CT angiography) shows a wedge-shaped perfusion defect; noncontrast CT for stones is normal. Treat with anticoagulation (heparin, then long-term oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation); catheter-directed therapy is reserved for selected early, complete occlusions.

Atheroembolic kidney disease

Kidney function that worsens over days to weeks after catheterisation, with livedo and eosinophilia, is atheroembolic disease, whereas contrast-associated injury appears within 24–72 hours and usually recovers within a week. Treatment is supportive: blood pressure control, statin, aspirin, avoidance of further arterial procedures and, if possible, anticoagulation; dialysis if needed. There is no proven role for glucocorticoids.

Scleroderma renal crisis

Abrupt hypertension (sometimes normotensive), rising creatinine and often microangiopathic hemolysis in a patient with early diffuse systemic sclerosis: start a short-acting ACE inhibitor (captopril) and titrate quickly, continuing it even when creatinine rises or dialysis is needed, because many patients recover enough to stop dialysis. Avoid high-dose glucocorticoids in at-risk patients. Prophylactic ACE inhibitors are not recommended.

Renal vein thrombosis

Diagnose with Doppler ultrasonography, CT or MR venography. Treat acute thrombosis with anticoagulation, continued while the nephrotic syndrome persists. In membranous nephropathy with serum albumin very low (well below about 2.5 g/dL) and low bleeding risk, prophylactic anticoagulation is sometimes considered.

Exam trap: in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis the next step is almost always optimal medical therapy, not stenting. The question often hides one of the few revascularisation triggers, such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema.

s23c-s110601-2-1.bodyHtml:
Initial approach

Genitourinary injuries are evaluated after the primary survey. Gross hematuria, a pelvic fracture, blood at the urethral meatus, flank bruising or penetrating injury near the kidneys or pelvis prompts imaging. Hemodynamic stability decides whether a patient goes to imaging or straight to the operating room.

Urethral injury

  • Suspect it with blood at the meatus, inability to void, perineal or scrotal (butterfly) hematoma or a high-riding prostate.
  • Do not pass a urethral catheter first. A retrograde urethrogram comes before any catheter, because blind catheterisation can turn a partial tear into a complete one.
  • If the urethrogram shows disruption, drain the bladder with a suprapubic cystostomy. Repair is delayed (urethroplasty months later) or done by early endoscopic realignment in selected patients. Late complications: stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence.

Bladder injury

  • Diagnosis: CT cystography (or conventional retrograde cystography) with the bladder fully distended through a catheter (about 300–350 mL of contrast in adults). Standard CT with passive filling misses ruptures.
  • Extraperitoneal rupture: contrast around the bladder base in a flame pattern. Most are managed with catheter drainage for about 2 weeks and a cystogram before removal. Operate if the bladder neck is involved, bone fragments lie in the bladder, or the abdomen is being opened anyway.
  • Intraperitoneal rupture: contrast outlines bowel loops and fills the paracolic gutters. It needs surgical repair, because urine keeps leaking into the peritoneum.

Kidney injury

  • Imaging: contrast CT with delayed (excretory) images, which show the collecting system and urine leak. Indications in adults: gross hematuria, microscopic hematuria with hypotension, or a mechanism or examination that suggests renal injury (rapid deceleration, flank wound, lower rib fractures).
  • Grading (AAST) runs from I (contusion or small subcapsular hematoma) to V (shattered kidney or avulsion of the hilum, or devascularised kidney with active bleeding).
  • Management: most injuries, including many high-grade ones in stable patients, are managed nonoperatively with bed rest, serial hemoglobin and observation. Active contrast extravasation or a pseudoaneurysm in a stable or transiently responsive patient is treated with angioembolisation. Persistent hemodynamic instability, an expanding or pulsatile hematoma at laparotomy, or hilar avulsion needs exploration. Urine leaks often seal; persistent ones get a ureteral stent.

Ureteral injury

Usually iatrogenic. Recognised during surgery, it is repaired at once. Recognised later, it shows as flank pain, fever, ileus, rising creatinine, or watery vaginal discharge (ureterovaginal fistula). CT urography or retrograde pyelography confirms it; a stent or percutaneous nephrostomy diverts urine while it heals or until repair.

Exam trap: in a pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus, the next step is a retrograde urethrogram, not a Foley catheter and not a CT of the abdomen.

s23c-s110601-2-2.bodyHtml:
Urinary incontinence in practice

Start with history, a bladder diary, examination (including pelvic examination and cough stress test), urinalysis to exclude infection and hematuria, and a post-void residual when retention is possible. Look for reversible contributors: infection, atrophic vaginitis, drugs (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics, alpha blockers in women), constipation, excess fluid or caffeine, poor mobility and hyperglycemia.

TypeFirst lineNext steps
StressPelvic floor muscle training, weight lossVaginal pessary or urethral insert; midurethral sling; bulking agents
Urge (overactive bladder)Bladder training (scheduled, gradually lengthened voiding), fluid and caffeine adjustment, pelvic floor trainingBeta-3 agonist or antimuscarinic; then intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA, sacral neuromodulation or tibial nerve stimulation
MixedTreat the most bothersome part firstCombine approaches
OverflowTreat the cause (stop offending drugs, alpha blocker for prostatic obstruction)Clean intermittent catheterisation for an underactive detrusor
FunctionalPrompted or scheduled toileting, mobility aids, bedside commodeAddress cognition, environment and caregiving

In older adults, strongly anticholinergic drugs (oxybutynin especially) can cause confusion, constipation, dry mouth and falls, and add to the anticholinergic burden in dementia; a beta-3 agonist is preferred when a drug is needed. Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so check it on treatment.

Neurogenic bladder

  • Underactive detrusor or large residual (spina bifida, cauda equina, diabetic neuropathy): clean intermittent catheterisation every 4–6 hours is preferred over an indwelling catheter.
  • Overactive detrusor with dyssynergia (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis): antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist plus intermittent catheterisation; intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA if needed. Monitor kidney function and the upper tracts with ultrasound because of the high pressures.
  • Autonomic dysreflexia: sit the patient up, loosen tight clothing and look for the trigger, usually a blocked catheter or full bladder; drain it. Treat severe persistent hypertension with a fast-acting agent such as nitrates if there is no recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use.

Obstruction

  • Acute urinary retention (often prostatic enlargement with an anticholinergic or decongestant trigger): drain with a urethral catheter (suprapubic if that fails), start an alpha-1 blocker, and attempt a trial without catheter after a few days.
  • Hydronephrosis on ultrasound with rising creatinine: find the level. Bilateral hydronephrosis with a distended bladder means outlet obstruction (catheter first); unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis with an empty bladder means ureteral obstruction (stent or nephrostomy).
  • Post-obstructive diuresis: after decompression, monitor urine output, vital signs and electrolytes closely. Replace fluids with a hypotonic or isotonic solution at less than the urine output (for example about half), so as not to drive the diuresis.

Vesicoureteral reflux

Reflux of urine from bladder to ureter through an incompetent ureterovesical junction (primary: short intramural ureter; secondary: high bladder pressure from valves or neurogenic bladder). It predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal scarring. Graded I (ureter only) to V (gross dilation and tortuosity of the ureter and pelvis with blunted calyces) on voiding cystourethrography.

  • After a first febrile UTI in a child aged 2–24 months, obtain renal and bladder ultrasonography. Voiding cystourethrography follows if ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, scarring or other findings that suggest high-grade reflux or obstruction, or after a second febrile UTI.
  • Low grades often resolve with growth. Management includes treating bladder and bowel dysfunction (constipation), prompt treatment of febrile UTIs, continuous antibiotic prophylaxis for selected children (for example higher grades or recurrent infection), and surgery (ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic injection) for breakthrough infections, high grades that persist or new scarring.

Enuresis

  • Primary nocturnal enuresis (never dry, older than 5 years): reassurance, then a bed-wetting alarm (most durable) or oral desmopressin (restrict evening fluids to avoid hyponatremia).
  • Secondary enuresis (wetting again after at least 6 months dry): look for a cause: UTI, constipation, new-onset diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus (urinalysis for glucose and specific gravity), obstructive sleep apnea, psychosocial stress and, when suspected, abuse.

Other mechanical disorders

  • Urethral diverticulum (women): a tender anterior vaginal wall mass, post-void dribbling, dysuria, dyspareunia and recurrent UTI; pus may be expressed from the meatus. MRI of the pelvis is the most accurate test; symptomatic diverticula are excised.
  • Pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, uterine or vaginal vault prolapse, rectocele): pressure, a vaginal bulge, voiding difficulty and incomplete emptying. Treat only if symptomatic: pelvic floor training, a pessary, or surgical repair. A large prolapse can kink the urethra and cause retention or even hydronephrosis.

s23c-s110701-2-1.bodyHtml:
Prenatal hydronephrosis

Dilation of the renal pelvis is the commonest anomaly found on prenatal ultrasonography. Most mild dilation resolves. After birth:

  • Unilateral hydronephrosis with a normal bladder: renal and bladder ultrasonography after about 48 hours of life (and within the first weeks). Earlier scans underestimate dilation because newborns are relatively oliguric in the first 1–2 days.
  • Bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick bladder or a dilated posterior urethra in a boy, or oligohydramnios: suspect posterior urethral valves. Scan in the first day, place a urethral catheter, and obtain voiding cystourethrography.
  • Persistent or worsening dilation leads to voiding cystourethrography (reflux, valves) and a diuretic renal scan (MAG3 with furosemide), which measures split function and drainage.

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction

  • Ultrasonography: dilated pelvis and calyces with a non-dilated ureter.
  • Diuretic renography: delayed drainage after furosemide indicates obstruction; split function is measured at the same time.
  • Many infants are watched with serial ultrasound. Pyeloplasty (open, laparoscopic or robotic dismembered pyeloplasty) is offered for symptoms (pain, infection, stones), reduced split function (often below about 40%), falling function on follow-up or worsening dilation.

Multicystic dysplastic kidney

Ultrasound shows noncommunicating cysts without normal parenchyma; a renal scan confirms no function. Management is conservative: serial ultrasonography to confirm involution and growth of the other kidney, and evaluation of the contralateral kidney, which has reflux or ureteropelvic junction obstruction in a meaningful share of children (voiding cystourethrography if it is dilated or the child has a febrile UTI). Nephrectomy is reserved for rare complications such as a large mass effect, hypertension or a solid component.

Bilateral agenesis and lethal oligohydramnios

Absent kidneys and bladder with anhydramnios at the mid-trimester anatomy scan predict lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. Counsel the family about the prognosis and the options (continuing with perinatal palliative care or ending the pregnancy), with support and genetic evaluation, because some forms recur.

Duplex systems and ectopic ureter

A girl who is wet all day and night yet also voids normally has an ectopic ureter until proven otherwise. Renal and bladder ultrasonography usually shows a duplex kidney with a dilated upper pole; MRI urography or cystoscopy locates the opening. Treatment is surgical (upper-pole heminephrectomy if that moiety does not function, or ureteral reimplantation or ureteroureterostomy). A ureterocele may be punctured endoscopically.

Horseshoe and pelvic kidney

Usually found incidentally and need no treatment. Children with Turner syndrome should have renal ultrasonography at diagnosis because of the frequent horseshoe kidney and collecting-system anomalies. Ectopic kidneys complicate trauma, abdominal aortic surgery and transplant surgery planning.

Urachal remnants

A newborn with persistent clear, urine-like drainage from the umbilicus may have a patent urachus; a fluid creatinine much higher than serum supports it. Ultrasonography of the umbilical region and bladder is the first test, with voiding cystourethrography to exclude bladder outlet obstruction, which can keep the urachus open. Symptomatic remnants are excised to prevent infection and later malignancy.

Bladder exstrophy

Diagnosed at birth (or prenatally by a non-visualised bladder with a low umbilical cord insertion). Cover the bladder plate with plastic wrap and refer for staged reconstruction; long-term issues are continence, fertility, upper-tract protection and cancer surveillance.

Exam trap: a newborn ultrasound on the first day after mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis can falsely reassure. Wait about 48 hours unless bilateral disease or a male infant with suspected valves needs earlier assessment.

s23c-s110801-2-1.bodyHtml:
Recognising drug-related kidney injury

Review every drug, including over-the-counter NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, supplements and recent contrast, whenever creatinine rises. The urine sediment and the time course usually point to the mechanism.

PatternTypical drugsCluesManagement
Hemodynamic (prerenal)NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, diuretics, calcineurin inhibitorsBland sediment, BUN:creatinine above 20, low urine sodium; often a volume-depleted older patientHold the offending drugs, restore volume, recheck
Acute tubular necrosisAminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, contrastMuddy brown granular casts, urine sodium above 40 mEq/L, FENa above 2%; aminoglycoside injury is nonoliguric and appears after 5–10 daysStop or dose-adjust, monitor levels, replace magnesium and potassium, avoid other nephrotoxins
Acute interstitial nephritisBeta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, immune checkpoint inhibitorsSterile pyuria, white cell casts, sometimes rash, fever or eosinophiliaStop the drug; corticosteroids if no prompt recovery. For checkpoint inhibitors: hold the drug and start prednisone for moderate or worse injury
Crystal nephropathyIV acyclovir, methotrexate, sulfadiazine, indinavirCrystals in urine, AKI within days of a high doseHydrate, stop or reduce the drug; for methotrexate, leucovorin, alkalinisation and glucarpidase if severe
Pseudo-AKI (creatinine secretion blocked)Trimethoprim, cimetidine; some kinase inhibitorsCreatinine up about 10–30% within days, BUN unchanged, bland urine; cystatin C unchangedNo change needed if this is the only finding; watch potassium with trimethoprim

ACE inhibitors and ARBs: when a creatinine rise is acceptable

Check creatinine and potassium within about 2–4 weeks of starting or increasing the dose. A rise of up to about 30% that then stabilises is expected and the drug should be continued, because it reflects the intended fall in intraglomerular pressure. A larger rise calls for a search for volume depletion, NSAIDs or renal artery stenosis and dose reduction or a pause. Manage mild hyperkalemia with dietary advice, stopping potassium supplements, a diuretic or a potassium binder before abandoning the drug.

Iodinated contrast

  • Do not withhold a clinically necessary contrast study because of kidney function; the risk is small and mostly confined to eGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73 m² (or AKI).
  • For high-risk patients who are not volume overloaded: IV isotonic crystalloid before and after, the lowest needed dose of a low- or iso-osmolar agent, and pausing NSAIDs and diuretics where safe.
  • N-acetylcysteine and prophylactic dialysis do not help. Metformin is held after contrast in patients with eGFR below 30 or AKI.

Gadolinium

In eGFR below 30 or dialysis, use a lower-risk (macrocyclic, group II) agent at the lowest dose only when the information is needed; for patients already on hemodialysis, dialysis soon after the scan is commonly arranged.

Specific drugs

  • Aminoglycosides: once-daily dosing, trough monitoring, shortest course; avoid with loop diuretics, vancomycin, contrast and NSAIDs where possible.
  • Cisplatin: prehydrate with saline and give magnesium. Hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia refractory (magnesium normally restrains potassium secretion through ROMK), so replace magnesium first or together with potassium.
  • Lithium: monitor levels, creatinine, calcium and TSH. For nephrogenic DI when lithium must continue, add amiloride; thiazides also reduce polyuria but raise lithium levels.
  • Tenofovir: monitor creatinine, urine glucose and protein and phosphate on TDF; switch to tenofovir alafenamide or another regimen if tubulopathy appears.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab): AIN is the usual kidney lesion, often weeks to months in and often with a PPI or NSAID as co-trigger. Exclude other causes, hold the inhibitor and give prednisone for moderate or worse injury; rechallenge may be possible once recovered, after discussion with oncology.
  • Cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide: hydration and mesna to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis; evaluate later hematuria for bladder cancer.

Drug-induced urinary retention

Suspect it in an older man with prostatic enlargement who has just started an antihistamine, antimuscarinic, tricyclic, decongestant or opioid, or after anesthesia. Confirm with a bladder scan (post-void residual). Decompress the bladder with a urethral catheter (suprapubic catheter if urethral placement fails or is contraindicated), stop the drug, and in men start an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin before a trial without catheter.

Exam trap: a creatinine rise of about 0.2–0.3 mg/dL a few days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with an unchanged BUN and bland urine is blocked creatinine secretion, not kidney injury. Stopping the antibiotic is not needed for that reason alone.

s23c-s150101-2-1.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

TestDiabetesPrediabetes
Hemoglobin A1c6.5% or higher5.7–6.4%
Fasting plasma glucose (8 h or more without calories)126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher100–125 mg/dL
2-hour glucose on a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher140–199 mg/dL
Random glucose with classic symptoms or a hyperglycemic crisis200 mg/dL or higher—

Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis needs two abnormal results: two different tests from the same sample, or the same test repeated. If two tests disagree, repeat the test that was abnormal. A1c is unreliable when red cell lifespan is altered (hemolysis, recent bleeding or transfusion, pregnancy, iron deficiency, hemoglobin variants, advanced CKD); use glucose-based tests then.

Screening

  • USPSTF: adults aged 35–70 with overweight or obesity, every 3 years if normal.
  • ADA: everyone from age 35, and earlier in adults with overweight or obesity plus a risk factor (first-degree relative, high-risk ethnicity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, polycystic ovary syndrome, inactivity, history of gestational diabetes).
  • Prediabetes: intensive lifestyle programme aiming for about 7% weight loss and 150 minutes a week of activity; metformin can be considered in younger, heavier patients or after gestational diabetes.

Treating type 2 diabetes

  1. Lifestyle for everyone: nutrition therapy, activity, weight loss; diabetes self-management education.
  2. Choose drugs by comorbidity first, then by glucose and weight goals.
    • Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or high risk: a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit, regardless of A1c.
    • Heart failure (reduced or preserved ejection fraction): an SGLT2 inhibitor.
    • CKD with albuminuria or reduced eGFR: an SGLT2 inhibitor (and RAS blockade); a GLP-1 receptor agonist if more glucose lowering is needed.
    • Obesity: a GLP-1 receptor agonist or tirzepatide gives the most weight loss.
    • Metformin remains a sound, cheap foundation when none of these drives the choice.
  3. Add or intensify every 3 months if the individual A1c target is not reached. Consider insulin early when A1c is above 10%, glucose is 300 mg/dL or higher, or there is catabolism (weight loss) or symptomatic hyperglycemia.
  4. Insulin: start basal insulin at about 10 units a day or 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day and titrate by a few units every few days until fasting glucose is at target. If fasting glucose is controlled but A1c is still high, add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or prandial insulin rather than pushing basal insulin ever higher.

Targets

  • A1c below 7% for many nonpregnant adults; tighter if achievable without hypoglycemia; less strict (for example below 8.0%) in older adults with multiple illnesses, cognitive impairment or limited life expectancy, in whom hypoglycemia causes falls and harm. Stop or avoid sulfonylureas (especially glyburide) and deintensify when glucose is overtreated.
  • Blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg for most; ACE inhibitor or ARB when there is albuminuria.
  • Statin: at least moderate intensity for ages 40–75; high intensity with ASCVD or multiple risk factors.
  • Aspirin for secondary prevention; for primary prevention only after weighing bleeding risk.

Complication surveillance

CheckType 1Type 2
Dilated eye examinationWithin 5 years of onset, then every 1–2 yearsAt diagnosis, then every 1–2 years if normal
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFRYearly from 5 years after onsetAt diagnosis, then at least yearly

Diabetic foot: a neuropathic plantar ulcer heals only with offloading (total contact cast or removable walker), debridement and good perfusion; check pulses and the ankle-brachial index. s23c-s150101-2-2.bodyHtml:
Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

DKA: glucose above about 200 mg/dL (or known diabetes), ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate raised) and acidosis (pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L), with a raised anion gap. Precipitants: missed insulin, infection, new-onset type 1, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, SGLT2 inhibitors, cocaine. HHS: glucose usually above 600 mg/dL, markedly raised osmolality (total osmolality classically above about 320 mOsm/kg), little ketosis or acidosis, and often altered mental status.

Management (same backbone for both)

  1. Fluids first: isotonic saline (or a balanced crystalloid) about 1–1.5 L in the first hour, then guided by volume status and the corrected sodium. Patients with HHS have the larger deficit.
  2. Potassium before insulin decisions:
    • K+ below 3.3 mEq/L: hold insulin and give IV potassium until 3.3 or higher; insulin would drive K+ into cells and risk arrhythmia.
    • 3.3–5.0 mEq/L: add potassium to each litre of fluid.
    • Above 5.0 mEq/L: no potassium yet; recheck every 1–2 hours.
  3. Insulin: continuous IV regular insulin (about 0.1 units/kg/hour). In mild DKA, subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin is an alternative.
  4. Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 mg/dL in DKA (about 300 mg/dL in HHS) and continue insulin until the ketoacidosis resolves. In DKA, insulin is being given to clear ketones, not just to lower glucose.
  5. Bicarbonate only for severe acidemia (pH below about 7.0). Phosphate only if severely low.
  6. Transition when the anion gap has closed and the patient can eat: give subcutaneous basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping the infusion to avoid rebound ketoacidosis.
  7. Monitor glucose hourly and electrolytes every 2–4 hours; look for and treat the precipitant. Lower glucose and sodium gradually, particularly in children, to reduce the risk of cerebral edema.

Sick-day rules

  • Type 1 diabetes: never stop basal insulin, even when not eating; check glucose every 2–4 hours and ketones when glucose is high or vomiting occurs; drink carbohydrate-containing fluids if not eating; seek care for persistent vomiting, moderate or large ketones, or confusion.
  • Pause SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs during dehydrating illness. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors at least 3 days before planned surgery.

Type 1 diabetes and pregnancy planning

Hyperglycemia at conception and in the first trimester raises the risk of miscarriage and congenital anomalies (cardiac defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression). Before conception: reliable contraception until glucose is controlled, an A1c below 6.5% if this can be reached without significant hypoglycemia, folic acid, a dilated eye examination, and stopping teratogenic drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs and statins. Insulin needs fall slightly in the first trimester and rise steeply in the second and third.

Exam trap: "the glucose is now 220 mg/dL, so stop the insulin drip" is wrong in DKA. Add dextrose and keep the insulin running until the anion gap closes.

s23c-s150102-2-1.bodyHtml:
Treat first

Hypoglycemia is treated before it is explained.

SituationTreatment
Awake and able to swallow15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets or gel, juice, regular soda); recheck glucose after 15 minutes and repeat if still low; then a snack or meal once glucose is normal
Unable to swallow safely, no IV access (home, community)Glucagon: intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, or intranasal powder; turn the person on their side because vomiting is common. Never put food or fluid in the mouth of a person who cannot swallow.
Hospital with IV accessIV dextrose bolus, then a dextrose infusion if the cause is long-acting

Glucagon works only if liver glycogen is present, so it may fail in starvation, alcohol-related hypoglycemia and advanced liver disease. Anyone treated with insulin, or with a history of level 2 or 3 hypoglycemia, should have glucagon prescribed and family members taught to use it.

Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia

Sulfonylureas, especially long-acting agents and those cleared by the kidney (glyburide), cause prolonged and recurrent hypoglycemia, most of all in older adults and in chronic kidney disease. Dextrose alone can make it worse, because each glucose bolus stimulates more insulin release. Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, inhibits insulin secretion and prevents recurrence. Patients are admitted for monitoring because the drug effect can outlast a day. In older adults with diabetes, avoid long-acting sulfonylureas and relax glycemic targets.

Hypoglycemia unawareness

Repeated hypoglycemia in long-standing type 1 diabetes blunts the glucagon response and lowers the glucose level that triggers adrenergic warning symptoms, so the first sign may be confusion or a seizure. Management: continuous glucose monitoring with alerts, review of insulin doses, and a period of strict avoidance of hypoglycemia with temporarily higher glucose targets, which partly restores awareness over weeks. Automated insulin delivery systems further reduce hypoglycemia.

Evaluating hypoglycemia in a person without diabetes

  1. Confirm Whipple's triad. A healthy-looking person with vague symptoms and a normal glucose during symptoms needs no further testing.
  2. Look for an obvious cause: drugs (including access to a relative's diabetes medicines), alcohol, critical illness, adrenal insufficiency, a large tumour.
  3. Draw blood during hypoglycemia (spontaneous, or provoked by a supervised fast of up to 72 hours, or a mixed-meal test if symptoms follow meals): glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides; insulin antibodies if insulin is very high. At the end of the fast, glucagon is given: a brisk glucose rise shows that insulin had kept glycogen in the liver.
  4. Localise only after biochemistry proves endogenous hyperinsulinism with a negative drug screen: multiphase contrast CT or MRI of the pancreas, then endoscopic ultrasonography; specialised functional imaging or selective arterial calcium stimulation for small tumours that remain hidden.

Management of the causes

  • Insulinoma: surgical removal (enucleation or partial pancreatectomy) cures most patients. Diazoxide, which opens beta-cell potassium channels and inhibits insulin release, or a somatostatin analogue controls symptoms when surgery is not possible.
  • Post-bariatric hypoglycemia: dietary change first: small, frequent meals with protein and fat and few rapidly absorbed carbohydrates; acarbose next; specialist options after that.
  • Factitious hypoglycemia (secret use of insulin or a secretagogue): share the results with the patient privately and without blame, and offer psychiatric care. Check for a pharmacy dispensing error before assuming deliberate use.
  • Adrenal insufficiency: glucocorticoid replacement.
  • Neonates at risk (infant of a mother with diabetes, large or small for gestational age, preterm): check glucose in the first hours; early feeding, oral dextrose gel, and IV dextrose if low glucose persists or the infant has symptoms.

Exam trap: do not start imaging the pancreas in a patient with hypoglycemia until insulin-mediated hypoglycemia has been proven and a sulfonylurea screen is negative.

s23c-s150201-2-1.bodyHtml:
Testing strategy

  • Start with TSH. If abnormal, add free T4 (and total or free T3 when TSH is suppressed but free T4 is normal, to find T3 toxicosis).
  • When pituitary or hypothalamic disease is known or suspected, TSH is misleading: measure free T4 and follow free T4 on treatment.
  • Antibodies: anti-TPO supports Hashimoto (and predicts progression of subclinical hypothyroidism); TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb or TSI) confirm Graves.
  • Radioactive iodine uptake and scan sorts thyrotoxicosis once TSH is suppressed: diffuse high uptake (Graves), patchy uptake (toxic multinodular goiter), one hot nodule with the rest suppressed (toxic adenoma), and low uptake (thyroiditis, exogenous hormone, recent iodine load). Serum thyroglobulin is low with exogenous hormone and high with thyroiditis.

Hypothyroidism

  • Treatment: levothyroxine, about 1.6 µg/kg/day in a healthy adult; start low (25–50 µg) in older adults or with coronary disease. Recheck TSH 6–8 weeks after each change.
  • Absorption: take on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast. Calcium, iron, proton pump inhibitors, bile acid sequestrants, sucralfate and some fibres reduce absorption; separate them by about 4 hours. Estrogen raises TBG and dose needs; enzyme inducers raise clearance.
  • Pregnancy: requirements rise early. A woman already on levothyroxine increases her dose by roughly 25–30% (for example two extra doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, with TSH checked about every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy.
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal free T4): repeat TSH with free T4 in about 2–3 months, because many values normalise. Treat persistent TSH of 10 mU/L or more; for lower values, treatment is individualised (symptoms, positive anti-TPO, pregnancy or plans for pregnancy). The normal TSH range shifts upward with age, so older adults with mild elevation are usually observed.
  • Myxedema coma: decompensated hypothyroidism, often triggered by infection, cold or sedatives, with hypothermia, depressed consciousness, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation (hypercapnia), hyponatremia and hypoglycemia. Give IV glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) first or together with IV levothyroxine until adrenal insufficiency is excluded (thyroid hormone raises cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis), plus ventilatory support, passive rewarming and correction of sodium and glucose in an ICU.

Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis

  • Symptom control: a β-blocker (propranolol, atenolol) for palpitations, tremor and anxiety, unless contraindicated.
  • Graves: three options. Methimazole for 12–18 months (lasting remission in roughly a third to a half); radioactive iodine (definitive, then lifelong levothyroxine); thyroidectomy (large goiter with compression, suspicious nodule, moderate-to-severe active orbitopathy, pregnancy planned soon, or patient preference). Avoid radioiodine in pregnancy, breastfeeding and moderate-to-severe active orbitopathy; if radioiodine is chosen with mild active orbitopathy, give glucocorticoid cover. Stop smoking.
  • Pregnancy: PTU in the first trimester (methimazole embryopathy); switch to methimazole afterwards (PTU hepatotoxicity). Aim for free T4 at the upper end of normal with the lowest dose.
  • Thionamide toxicity: fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers mean agranulocytosis until proven otherwise: stop the drug and check a CBC with differential. Do not switch to the other thionamide (cross-reactivity). Check liver tests for jaundice or right upper quadrant pain.
  • Toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter: radioiodine or surgery; thionamides control but do not cure.
  • Thyroiditis: β-blocker only; NSAIDs (or prednisone if severe) for painful subacute thyroiditis; no thionamides; watch for the hypothyroid phase.
  • Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T4 and T3): treat when TSH is below about 0.1 mU/L in patients 65 or older, or with heart disease, osteoporosis or symptoms; otherwise monitor.
  • Thyroid storm: life-threatening thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, delirium and GI or hepatic dysfunction, often triggered by infection, surgery or iodine. In order: β-blocker (propranolol); thionamide (PTU preferred, as it also blocks conversion); iodine solution at least 1 hour after the thionamide; hydrocortisone; cooling with acetaminophen (avoid aspirin, which frees hormone from TBG); treat the trigger in an ICU.

Exam trap: in hypopituitarism, a "normal" TSH on levothyroxine says nothing. Titrate to free T4 in the upper half of normal.

s23c-s150201-2-2.bodyHtml:
Thyroid nodules

Nodules are very common, especially in older women, and most are benign. The approach:

  1. TSH first. If TSH is low, do a radionuclide scan: a hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule is almost never malignant and needs no biopsy; treat the hyperthyroidism.
  2. Otherwise, neck ultrasonography of the thyroid and cervical nodes. High-risk features: solid hypoechoic nodule, irregular or infiltrative margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, extrathyroidal extension, suspicious nodes.
  3. Fine-needle aspiration by sonographic pattern and size: high or intermediate suspicion at 1 cm or more; low suspicion at about 1.5 cm or more; very low suspicion (spongiform) at about 2 cm or more, or observation. Purely cystic nodules are not biopsied. Abnormal lymph nodes are sampled directly.
Bethesda categoryMeaningUsual next step
INondiagnosticRepeat ultrasound-guided FNA
IIBenignUltrasound follow-up (interval set by the sonographic pattern); repeat FNA if it grows significantly or the pattern is high suspicion
III and IVAtypia of undetermined significance; follicular neoplasmRepeat FNA or molecular testing; diagnostic lobectomy when risk stays high
V and VISuspicious for malignancy; malignantSurgery

Differentiated thyroid cancer, in outline

  • Papillary and follicular cancers are treated with surgery (lobectomy for many small low-risk tumours; total thyroidectomy for larger, multifocal or node-positive disease), selective radioiodine ablation after total thyroidectomy for higher-risk disease, and TSH suppression tailored to risk. Thyroglobulin is the tumour marker after total thyroidectomy.
  • Very small, low-risk papillary microcarcinomas may be managed by active surveillance in selected patients.
  • Medullary cancer: test for RET germline variants and exclude pheochromocytoma before surgery (MEN2); total thyroidectomy; follow calcitonin and CEA. Radioiodine is useless.
  • Anaplastic cancer and lymphoma both present as a rapidly enlarging neck mass with compressive symptoms; core biopsy distinguishes them because treatment differs completely.

Nonthyroidal illness in hospital

Critically ill patients often have low T3, low or normal T4 and low or normal TSH. Do not order thyroid tests in the ICU without strong suspicion of thyroid disease, and do not treat these values; repeat after recovery. Dopamine and high-dose glucocorticoids also suppress TSH.

Drug effects to recognise

  • Amiodarone: check TSH before starting and every few months. Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine and the amiodarone often continued. Thyrotoxicosis: type 1 (iodine-driven synthesis) responds to thionamides; type 2 (destructive) responds to glucocorticoids; mixed forms get both.
  • Lithium: goiter and hypothyroidism; treat with levothyroxine and usually continue lithium.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors: painless thyroiditis (transient thyrotoxicosis then hypothyroidism) and hypophysitis (central hypothyroidism with central adrenal insufficiency).
  • Iodinated contrast in a patient with nodular goiter can trigger thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow).
  • Biotin supplements interfere with many immunoassays and can mimic Graves (low TSH, high free T4); stop biotin for a few days and repeat.

Exam trap: a benign FNA does not end follow-up, and a hot nodule on scan does not need FNA. Order of thinking: TSH, then scan or ultrasound, then FNA by pattern.

s23c-s150301-2-1.bodyHtml:
Hypercalcemia: work-up and management

  1. Confirm: repeat calcium with albumin, or measure ionised calcium.
  2. Measure intact PTH. High or inappropriately normal: primary hyperparathyroidism versus FHH (24-hour urine calcium and creatinine; calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 suggests FHH). Suppressed: measure PTHrP, 25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains, and look for cancer.

Acute severe hypercalcemia (usually above 14 mg/dL, or any level with confusion): give intravenous isotonic saline to restore volume, because hypercalcemia causes a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and volume depletion that further reduce calcium excretion. Add calcitonin for a fast but short-lived fall (tachyphylaxis within about 2 days), and an intravenous bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) for a sustained effect over 2–4 days. Denosumab is an option when kidney function precludes bisphosphonates. Loop diuretics are used only after volume is restored, if fluid overload develops. Glucocorticoids treat calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (granulomatous disease, lymphoma). Hemodialysis is for life-threatening hypercalcemia with kidney failure.

Primary hyperparathyroidism

Most patients are found on routine testing and have no symptoms. Parathyroidectomy by an experienced surgeon is the only cure and is recommended for anyone with symptoms (stones, fractures, symptomatic hypercalcemia). In asymptomatic patients, surgery is advised when any of the following is present:

  • serum calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal;
  • osteoporosis by DXA (T-score −2.5 or less at any site) or a vertebral fracture on imaging;
  • eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis, or high urinary calcium excretion;
  • age below 50 years.

Imaging (sestamibi scan, neck ultrasonography, 4D-CT) localises an adenoma once the decision to operate is made; it does not make the diagnosis, which is biochemical. Patients who do not meet criteria or decline surgery are monitored with yearly calcium and creatinine and periodic DXA; cinacalcet lowers calcium, and a bisphosphonate protects bone, but neither cures the disease. Thiazides should be avoided because they raise calcium. After surgery, watch for hungry bone syndrome (falling calcium, phosphate and magnesium as the starved skeleton remineralises).

Secondary hyperparathyroidism (vitamin D deficiency, CKD) is a physiologic response to low calcium or high phosphate. In CKD, manage phosphate (diet, binders), replete 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and use calcitriol or a calcimimetic for progressive PTH elevation. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is autonomous gland hyperplasia after long-standing secondary disease, typically after kidney transplant, with hypercalcemia; treatment is parathyroidectomy or cinacalcet.

Exam trap: a sestamibi scan is not the next step for a new hypercalcemia. First prove the diagnosis biochemically and decide on surgery; image only to plan the operation.

s23c-s150301-2-2.bodyHtml:
Hypocalcemia: management

  • Severe or symptomatic (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, prolonged QT): intravenous calcium gluconate, then a continuous infusion with oral calcium and calcitriol. Check and replace magnesium first or at the same time.
  • Chronic hypoparathyroidism: oral calcium plus calcitriol (or alfacalcidol), because without PTH the kidney cannot make enough 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D from ordinary vitamin D. Aim for a low-normal serum calcium to limit hypercalciuria, stones and nephrocalcinosis; a thiazide can reduce urinary calcium. Recombinant PTH replacement is reserved for patients poorly controlled on conventional therapy.
  • Vitamin D deficiency: cholecalciferol (or ergocalciferol) replacement with adequate calcium intake.

Osteoporosis

Screening: DXA of the hip and lumbar spine for all women 65 years or older, and for younger postmenopausal women at increased risk (for example by FRAX or another risk tool). Evidence is insufficient to screen men routinely, although men with risk factors (glucocorticoids, hypogonadism, androgen deprivation therapy) are commonly assessed.

Diagnosis: T-score −2.5 or less at the femoral neck, total hip or lumbar spine; or a hip or vertebral fragility fracture regardless of T-score; or osteopenia (T-score between −1 and −2.5) with a high 10-year FRAX fracture probability. Look for secondary causes: glucocorticoids, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, celiac disease, myeloma, chronic kidney or liver disease, alcohol use, aromatase inhibitors.

Treatment:

s23c-s150401-2-1.bodyHtml:
Adrenal insufficiency

  • Diagnose: an early-morning serum cortisol with plasma ACTH. A very low cortisol (below about 3–5 µg/dL) strongly suggests insufficiency; a clearly normal value (above about 15–18 µg/dL) makes it unlikely. Confirm with the cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test: a peak cortisol below about 18 µg/dL (lower cut-offs, near 14–15 µg/dL, apply to newer specific assays) means insufficiency. High ACTH means primary; low or normal means secondary. In primary disease check 21-hydroxylase antibodies; if negative, image the adrenals (CT).
  • Treat primary insufficiency with hydrocortisone (split doses, the larger one on waking) plus fludrocortisone; secondary insufficiency needs glucocorticoid only. Teach sick-day rules: double or triple the oral dose during fever or illness, inject hydrocortisone intramuscularly if vomiting, give stress doses for surgery, and wear medical identification.
  • Adrenal crisis (hypotension or shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia): do not wait for test results. Draw cortisol and ACTH if it causes no delay, then give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately, followed by 200 mg per 24 hours, with rapid IV isotonic saline (and dextrose if hypoglycemic). Look for the precipitant (infection, missed doses).

Cushing syndrome

  1. Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid, including inhaled, topical, intra-articular and herbal products, and interactions with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
  2. Screen with a test that fits the patient: late-night salivary cortisol (at least two samples), the 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (morning cortisol above 1.8 µg/dL is abnormal), or 24-hour urine free cortisol (at least two collections). Use two abnormal tests to confirm. Estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin and gives false positives on the dexamethasone test; severe depression, alcohol use disorder and poorly controlled diabetes can mimic mild hypercortisolism.
  3. Measure plasma ACTH. Suppressed: adrenal CT. Normal or high (ACTH-dependent): pituitary MRI. A clear adenoma (about 10 mm or larger) with concordant tests points to Cushing disease; a small or absent lesion calls for bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH or desmopressin, where a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient identifies a pituitary source. No gradient: search for an ectopic source (CT chest and abdomen, functional imaging).
  4. Treat the source: transsphenoidal adenoma resection, adrenalectomy, or resection of the ectopic tumour. Medical options when surgery fails or must wait: steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat), the receptor blocker mifepristone, and pituitary-directed pasireotide or cabergoline. After successful surgery the remaining axis is suppressed, so glucocorticoid replacement is needed until it recovers.

Primary aldosteronism

  • Who to screen: current Endocrine Society guidance favours screening broadly, including adults with hypertension generally; it is clearly indicated with resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalemia (spontaneous or diuretic-induced), an adrenal incidentaloma, sleep apnea, atrial fibrillation, or a family history of early hypertension or stroke.
  • Screening test: morning plasma aldosterone with renin (activity or concentration). Suppressed renin with an inappropriately high aldosterone is positive. Correct hypokalemia first (it lowers aldosterone). Mineralocorticoid antagonists and diuretics can raise renin and mask the diagnosis.
  • Confirm (for example, with saline or oral sodium loading showing failure of aldosterone suppression) unless the result is unequivocal (spontaneous hypokalemia, renin suppressed, aldosterone very high).
  • Subtype: adrenal CT (mainly to exclude carcinoma), then adrenal vein sampling in a patient who wants surgery, because small nodules on CT are often nonfunctioning and bilateral disease is common, especially after about age 35–40.
  • Treat: unilateral disease, laparoscopic adrenalectomy; bilateral disease or a patient who declines surgery, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone, or eplerenone if gynecomastia or sexual side effects are a problem), titrated until renin is no longer suppressed.

s23c-s150401-2-2.bodyHtml:
Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma

  • Test: plasma free metanephrines (drawn supine after rest) or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines. Metanephrines are produced continuously inside the tumour, so they are more sensitive than catecholamines. Mild rises are common with tricyclic antidepressants, some antipsychotics, levodopa and sympathomimetics; levels several times the upper limit are highly specific.
  • Locate after biochemical confirmation: CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis (bright on T2-weighted MRI); functional imaging for extra-adrenal, multiple or metastatic disease.
  • Prepare for surgery with alpha blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin) for 1–2 weeks, with a high-sodium diet and fluids to restore volume. Add a beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade, for tachycardia. A beta blocker alone removes beta-2 vasodilation and leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can cause a hypertensive crisis.
  • After resection: watch for hypotension and hypoglycemia; offer genetic testing to every patient and lifelong biochemical follow-up.

Adrenal incidentaloma

Masses found on imaging done for another reason are common, especially in older adults. Two questions apply to every mass (see the figure):

  • Hormone excess: a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test for every patient (autonomous cortisol secretion is the most frequent finding); plasma or urine metanephrines unless the mass is clearly a lipid-rich adenoma (10 Hounsfield units or less on noncontrast CT), in which pheochromocytoma is very unlikely; aldosterone and renin if there is hypertension or hypokalemia.
  • Malignancy: a homogeneous mass with attenuation of 10 Hounsfield units or less on noncontrast CT is a lipid-rich adenoma. If it is under 4 cm and nonfunctioning, no further imaging is needed. Larger, heterogeneous or higher-attenuation masses need further imaging (contrast washout CT, MRI or FDG-PET) or surgery. Never biopsy before excluding pheochromocytoma; biopsy is reserved mainly for suspected metastasis when it would change management.
  • Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (cortisol not suppressed after dexamethasone without overt Cushing features) is linked to hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis and cardiovascular events; screen for these and treat them, and consider adrenalectomy case by case.

Puberty that comes early or late

Central (gonadotropin-dependent)Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent)
MechanismEarly activation of hypothalamic GnRH pulsesSex steroids from the adrenal, gonad, a tumour or outside source
LH (basal or after GnRH or GnRH-agonist stimulation)PubertalSuppressed
ExamplesIdiopathic (most girls); CNS lesions such as hypothalamic hamartoma, tumours, hydrocephalus, prior irradiation (more often in boys)Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome, ovarian cyst or tumour, Leydig cell tumour, hCG-secreting tumour, exogenous testosterone or estrogen
TreatmentGnRH agonist after brain MRI where indicatedTreat the source
  • Precocious puberty: secondary sexual characteristics before about age 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Start with growth velocity and bone age (advanced in true puberty). Brain MRI is indicated in all boys with central precocious puberty and in younger girls (under about 6 years) or any child with neurologic signs. Testicular enlargement points to central puberty or a Leydig cell tumour (unilateral); prepubertal testes with virilisation point to an adrenal source.
  • McCune-Albright syndrome: a postzygotic activating GNAS variant (mosaic), giving peripheral precocious puberty from autonomous ovarian cysts, irregular "coast of Maine" café-au-lait macules and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, sometimes with other hormone excess.
  • Delayed puberty: no breast development by about 13 in girls, or testes under 4 mL by about 14 in boys. Constitutional delay is the most common cause (short with a delayed bone age, often a parent who matured late, normal growth velocity for bone age). Low LH and FSH also occur with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome with anosmia, pituitary disease, anorexia, chronic illness); high LH and FSH mean gonadal failure (Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome).

Exam trap: never start a beta blocker before alpha blockade in suspected pheochromocytoma, and never send a patient with suspected adrenal crisis for a stimulation test before giving hydrocortisone.

s23c-s150501-2-1.bodyHtml:
Approach to a sellar mass

Image with pituitary-protocol MRI. Test every patient with a macroadenoma for both hormone excess (prolactin, IGF-1, and a cortisol excess screen if Cushing features) and deficiency (8 AM cortisol, free T4 with TSH, LH, FSH and testosterone or estradiol). Check formal visual fields when the mass reaches the chiasm. An incidental microadenoma that secretes nothing is followed with repeat MRI; a nonfunctioning macroadenoma with visual loss goes to transsphenoidal surgery.

Hyperprolactinemia

CauseClue
Pregnancy, lactationAlways exclude pregnancy first
Drugs that block dopamineRisperidone, haloperidol, metoclopramide, domperidone; also verapamil, opioids; onset follows the drug
Primary hypothyroidismHigh TRH stimulates lactotrophs; the pituitary may enlarge (thyrotroph hyperplasia) and shrinks on levothyroxine
Kidney failure, cirrhosisReduced clearance
Stalk compressionNonfunctioning macroadenoma, craniopharyngioma; prolactin usually below about 100 ng/mL
ProlactinomaLevel roughly parallels tumour size
MacroprolactinBig, inactive prolactin-IgG complexes; high level, no symptoms

For a suspected drug cause, the safest step is to stop or switch the drug (for example from risperidone to aripiprazole, with the psychiatrist) and repeat the level; image if prolactin stays high or the drug cannot be changed.

Prolactinoma treatment: a dopamine agonist, usually cabergoline, is first line for symptomatic micro- and macroadenomas, even with visual field loss, because it shrinks most tumours within weeks. Surgery is for intolerance, resistance or apoplexy. An asymptomatic microadenoma in a woman who does not want pregnancy can simply be watched (or treated with a combined hormonal contraceptive for estrogen replacement). In pregnancy, a microadenoma rarely grows, and the agonist is usually stopped once pregnancy is confirmed; macroadenomas need closer follow-up with visual fields.

Acromegaly

  • Screen with serum IGF-1 (age- and sex-adjusted); a single GH level is useless because GH is pulsatile.
  • Confirm when IGF-1 is high or equivocal with an oral glucose tolerance test: GH fails to suppress (to below about 1 ng/mL).
  • Then pituitary MRI. Look for complications: colonoscopy, echocardiography, sleep study, glucose, blood pressure.
  • Treat with transsphenoidal surgery; if disease persists, a somatostatin receptor ligand (octreotide, lanreotide), pegvisomant, or a dopamine agonist for mild cases; radiotherapy for resistant tumours. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of excess mortality.

Pituitary apoplexy

Sudden severe headache, vomiting, visual loss or ophthalmoplegia, meningism and hypotension in a patient with (often unknown) adenoma. Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone immediately, before imaging results if necessary, because acute ACTH loss can kill. MRI (or CT if MRI is not available) confirms it; neurosurgical decompression is for severe or worsening visual loss or reduced consciousness.

Hypopituitarism

  • Causes: tumours and their treatment (surgery, radiation), apoplexy, Sheehan syndrome, trauma, infiltration (sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis), hypophysitis (including immune checkpoint inhibitors), empty sella.
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low or inappropriately normal ACTH with low cortisol; aldosterone is preserved (renin-angiotensin control), so hyperkalemia is absent.
  • Central hypothyroidism has a low free T4 with a low or normal TSH: follow free T4, not TSH, to adjust levothyroxine.
  • Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone. Levothyroxine speeds cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated ACTH deficiency.
  • Then sex steroids (or gonadotropins for fertility), GH in selected adults and children, and desmopressin if posterior deficiency.

Exam trap: in a patient with hypopituitarism, a normal TSH does not mean the thyroid is fine. Check free T4.

s23c-s150501-2-2.bodyHtml:
Polyuria: diabetes insipidus or not?

Polyuria is more than about 3 L/day in adults. First exclude osmotic diuresis (glucose), then measure plasma and urine osmolality and sodium together.

  • Dilute urine (below about 300 mOsm/kg) with high-normal or high serum sodium suggests diabetes insipidus.
  • Dilute urine with low-normal serum sodium suggests primary polydipsia.
  • Check calcium and potassium and ask about lithium (nephrogenic causes).

A water deprivation test separates the three; it ends with a dose of desmopressin. Where available, stimulated copeptin (copeptin is cleaved from the same precursor as ADH and is stable to measure, after hypertonic saline or arginine) separates primary polydipsia from central DI more accurately, and a high baseline copeptin points to nephrogenic DI.

Primary polydipsiaCentral DINephrogenic DI
Serum sodium at baselineLow-normalHigh-normal or highHigh-normal or high
Urine osmolality after deprivationRises wellStays lowStays low
Rise after desmopressinSmallLarge (often more than 50%)Little or none
TreatmentReduce intake; treat the causeDesmopressin; MRI for the causeRemove the cause; low-sodium, low-protein diet, thiazide; amiloride for lithium

Once central DI is confirmed, image the hypothalamus and pituitary to find the cause (tumour, infiltration, trauma, surgery). With desmopressin, the main risk is hyponatremia, so patients should drink only to thirst.

SIADH

Diagnose SIADH only after confirming hypotonic hyponatremia (low serum osmolality) in a clinically euvolemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine (above about 100 mOsm/kg) and urine sodium above about 30 mEq/L, and after excluding hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretics.

  • Severe symptoms (seizures, coma, vomiting with confusion): bolus 3% hypertonic saline.
  • Chronic or mild: fluid restriction first; then oral sodium chloride or urea; vaptans (V2 antagonists such as tolvaptan) in selected hospitalised patients with close sodium checks and not in liver disease.
  • Correction limit: in chronic hyponatremia raise sodium by no more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients (alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease) and about 10–12 in others, to avoid osmotic demyelination. If correction overshoots, give free water and desmopressin to bring sodium back down.
  • Isotonic saline can make SIADH hyponatremia worse: the salt is excreted in concentrated urine and the water is kept.

Short stature and growth hormone deficiency

Familial short statureConstitutional delayGH deficiency or other disease
Growth velocityNormalNormal (dips before a late growth spurt)Low
Bone ageEqual to chronological ageDelayedDelayed
FamilyShort parents; final height near targetA parent who matured lateVariable
ActionReassureReassure; reach normal adult heightIGF-1 (and IGFBP-3), then GH stimulation testing and MRI; recombinant GH

A child whose growth velocity falls (crossing percentiles downward) needs evaluation: check thyroid function, celiac serology, blood count, metabolic panel, and in girls a karyotype for Turner syndrome. Weight falling before height suggests a nutritional or systemic cause; height falling with weight preserved suggests an endocrine cause.

Exam trap: hyponatremia with a concentrated urine is not always SIADH. Low cortisol (secondary adrenal insufficiency) gives the identical lab picture and is fixed by hydrocortisone, not fluid restriction.

s23c-s1506-2-1.bodyHtml:
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea

  • A diagnosis of exclusion in a woman with amenorrhea of 3 months or more: exclude pregnancy first, then measure prolactin, TSH, FSH, LH and estradiol; check androgens if there are signs of hyperandrogenism (polycystic ovary syndrome). Image the pituitary if headache, visual change or unexplained low gonadotropins point to a lesion.
  • Typical pattern: low or low-normal LH and FSH, low estradiol, normal prolactin and TSH, in someone with energy deficit, weight loss, intense training or stress. Screen for an eating disorder.
  • Treatment is to correct the energy balance: increase calories, reduce training load, and give psychological support. Menses usually return with weight and energy restoration.
  • Measure bone density (DXA) if amenorrhea has lasted 6 months or more. Give adequate calcium and vitamin D. If menses do not return after an adequate trial of nutritional and behavioural treatment, short-term transdermal estradiol with cyclic oral progestin is suggested for bone protection. Combined oral contraceptives do not protect bone well in this setting and mask whether menses have returned, and bisphosphonates are avoided in young women who may become pregnant.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

  • Work-up: confirm low sex steroid with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH (testosterone measured fasting in the morning, twice). Check prolactin, iron studies (hemochromatosis), other pituitary axes, and ask about opioids, glucocorticoids, anabolic steroids and weight. Image the hypothalamus and pituitary when no functional cause explains it.
  • Opioid-induced: long-term opioids suppress GnRH; LH and testosterone are low. Options are tapering the opioid where possible, or testosterone replacement.
  • Treatment depends on fertility goals: testosterone (men) or estrogen with progestin (women) for puberty and bone; gonadotropins (hCG, adding FSH) or pulsatile GnRH when fertility is wanted. Exogenous testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis and must not be used for fertility.

Central precocious puberty

  • Pubertal signs before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys with accelerated growth and advanced bone age.
  • Central (gonadotropin-dependent): raised basal LH on a sensitive assay or an LH rise after GnRH-agonist stimulation. Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) causes have suppressed LH: congenital adrenal hyperplasia, ovarian or testicular tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome, exogenous steroids.
  • MRI of the brain for every boy with central precocious puberty and for girls who are very young (especially under 6) or have neurologic signs; boys more often have a lesion.
  • Treatment: a long-acting GnRH agonist (depot leuprolide, triptorelin, or a histrelin implant) to halt progression and preserve adult height, plus treatment of any underlying lesion. A hypothalamic hamartoma is usually managed medically unless seizures are refractory.

Central diabetes insipidus after sellar surgery

Polyuria with dilute urine and a rising sodium in the first days after transsphenoidal or hypothalamic surgery is central diabetes insipidus; treat with desmopressin while the patient drinks to thirst, and monitor sodium closely. A triphasic course can follow: DI, then a SIADH-like phase about a week later as damaged neurons release stored ADH, then permanent DI if most neurons are lost. Patients with impaired thirst need fixed fluid plans.

Exam trap: a man who wants children and has low testosterone from hypogonadotropic hypogonadism should get hCG, not testosterone. Testosterone shuts down LH and FSH and stops sperm production.

s23c-s1507-2-1.bodyHtml:
Who should be tested

  • Germline RET testing for every patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, even without a family history, and for anyone with features of MEN2 (bilateral or young-onset pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas).
  • Germline MEN1 testing for a patient with two or more of the main MEN1 tumours, primary hyperparathyroidism at a young age or with multigland disease, or a gastrinoma.
  • First-degree relatives of a person with a known pathogenic variant are offered targeted testing, after genetic counselling. Those who test negative need no further screening; carriers enter surveillance.

MEN2: the order of operations

  1. Before any operation in a patient with MTC or a RET variant, exclude pheochromocytoma with plasma free (or urine fractionated) metanephrines. An undiagnosed pheochromocytoma can cause a hypertensive crisis under anaesthesia.
  2. If a pheochromocytoma is present, give alpha-adrenergic blockade (for example phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 1–2 weeks, adding a beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade is established, with salt and fluid loading; then remove the adrenal tumour laparoscopically, preserving the cortex when the disease is bilateral where possible.
  3. Then perform total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection as indicated by tumour size, nodal disease and calcitonin.

Prophylactic thyroidectomy in carriers

Because MTC develops in nearly every carrier, children who inherit a RET variant have the thyroid removed before cancer spreads. The timing follows the variant's risk:

Risk classExampleTiming of total thyroidectomy
HighestM918T (MEN2B)In the first year of life
HighCodon 634At or before about 5 years, guided by calcitonin
ModerateOther codonsWhen calcitonin starts to rise, or in childhood if the family prefers not to wait

Carriers are also screened for pheochromocytoma (from late childhood in high-risk variants) and, in MEN2A, for hyperparathyroidism.

After thyroidectomy for MTC

  • Replace levothyroxine to a normal TSH, not a suppressed one.
  • Follow calcitonin and CEA; their doubling times predict progression. Thyroglobulin is not a marker for MTC.
  • Radioactive iodine is not used. Advanced, progressive disease is treated with systemic kinase inhibitors, including selective RET inhibitors, by specialists.

MEN1 management

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism: because all glands are hyperplastic, the operation is subtotal (three-and-a-half gland) parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation, plus transcervical thymectomy (supernumerary glands and thymic carcinoids). Removing one enlarged gland leads to persistence or early recurrence.
  • Gastrinoma: high-dose proton pump inhibitor controls acid; correcting hypercalcemia lowers gastrin; surgery is individualised because tumours are often multiple and small.
  • Prolactinoma: a dopamine agonist (cabergoline) first, as in sporadic disease.
  • Surveillance of carriers: periodic calcium and PTH, prolactin, fasting glucose and gastrin, chromogranin-related markers as used locally, and pancreatic and pituitary imaging at intervals.

Exam trap: in a patient with a RET variant or MTC, the first preoperative test is plasma metanephrines, and the first operation, if positive, is the adrenalectomy after alpha-blockade.

s23c-s150801-2-1.bodyHtml:
The newborn with atypical genitalia

  • Treat it as urgent: the most common cause, salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency, can cause adrenal crisis in the first weeks. Bilateral nonpalpable gonads in a virilised infant suggest a 46,XX infant with CAH until proven otherwise.
  • First tests: serum electrolytes and glucose, 17-hydroxyprogesterone (after the first 24–48 hours), rapid karyotype or sex-chromosome testing, pelvic and abdominal ultrasonography for a uterus and gonads; then testosterone, DHT, AMH, LH and FSH, and ACTH stimulation or genetic panels as needed.
  • Do not assign sex before the evaluation, and say so kindly to the family. Care is led by a multidisciplinary team (endocrinology, urology, genetics, psychology). Irreversible genital surgery is increasingly deferred where it is not medically necessary, so the person can take part in decisions.
  • Hypospadias with undescended testes, especially if either testis is nonpalpable or the hypospadias is proximal, warrants a DSD evaluation (karyotype, hormones) before any surgery; circumcision is postponed because the foreskin may be needed for repair.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

  • Newborn screening measures 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Levels are higher in preterm, sick or stressed infants and in samples taken in the first day, so screening cut-offs depend on gestational age or birth weight; a positive screen in a preterm infant is confirmed with serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (ideally by mass spectrometry) and electrolytes rather than treated immediately if the baby is well.
  • Salt-wasting crisis (vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia at 1–3 weeks): IV isotonic saline, dextrose and stress-dose hydrocortisone (for example about 50–100 mg/m² IV), then maintenance.
  • Maintenance: hydrocortisone (preferred in children because it is least suppressive of growth), fludrocortisone and, in infants, sodium chloride supplements. Monitor growth velocity, bone age, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androstenedione. Overtreatment slows growth; undertreatment advances bone age and causes early virilisation and short adult height.
  • Sick-day rules: double or triple the oral glucocorticoid dose for fever or illness; give intramuscular hydrocortisone and seek care if vomiting; fludrocortisone is not increased.

Congenital hypothyroidism

  • A raised screening TSH is confirmed with serum TSH and free T4. When the screening TSH is markedly high (around 40 mU/L or more) or free T4 is low, start levothyroxine 10–15 µg/kg/day as soon as the confirmatory blood is drawn, ideally within the first 2 weeks of life; imaging (ultrasonography or scintigraphy) is optional and must not delay treatment.
  • Give the tablet crushed in a little breast milk, formula or water by spoon; keep it apart from soy formula, iron and calcium, which reduce absorption. Recheck TSH and free T4 2 weeks after starting and then frequently in infancy, keeping free T4 in the upper half of the reference range.
  • If no permanent cause is shown, a trial off treatment after about age 3 can identify transient hypothyroidism.

Turner and Klinefelter syndromes: endocrine care

  • Turner syndrome: suspect with short stature, absent puberty or primary amenorrhea, lymphedema at birth, or a coarctation. At diagnosis: cardiac imaging (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, aortic dilation; risk of dissection), renal ultrasonography (horseshoe kidney), hearing and thyroid and celiac screening. Growth hormone for short stature; estrogen started around age 11–12 to induce puberty, with progestin added later.
  • Klinefelter syndrome: testosterone replacement for hypogonadism; infertility counselling (sperm retrieval from the testis is sometimes possible).

Exam trap: a 2-week-old boy with typical genitalia, vomiting, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia may have salt-wasting CAH; the normal genitalia hide the diagnosis, and pyloric stenosis gives the opposite electrolytes (hypokalemic, hypochloremic alkalosis).

s23c-s150901-2-1.bodyHtml:
Glucocorticoid therapy: safe use and withdrawal

  • Who is at risk of HPA suppression? Assume suppression after more than about 3 weeks of a supraphysiologic dose, with evening dosing, or with cushingoid features. Short courses (under 3 weeks) can usually be stopped without taper.
  • Tapering: reduce gradually toward a physiologic dose, then more slowly. If symptoms suggest insufficiency, a morning cortisol (taken 24 hours after the last hydrocortisone dose) helps decide whether the axis has recovered.
  • Stress dosing: patients on long-term glucocorticoids, or who stopped them recently, need extra doses during major surgery, severe illness or trauma. Teach sick-day rules (double or triple the dose during febrile illness), carry an emergency injection and wear medical identification.
  • Adrenal crisis (hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, confusion): give intravenous hydrocortisone immediately with isotonic saline and dextrose; draw cortisol and ACTH first if it does not delay treatment, but never wait for results.
  • Bone protection: for patients on 2.5 mg/day or more of prednisone for 3 months or longer, give calcium and vitamin D, assess fracture risk, and start a bisphosphonate when risk is moderate or high.
  • Hyperglycemia: prednisone given in the morning raises afternoon and evening glucose most; NPH insulin given with the morning steroid dose matches this pattern.

Thyroid effects of drugs: what to do

SituationFindingsManagement
Amiodarone, type 1 thyrotoxicosisNodular goiter or Graves disease; increased Doppler vascularity; uptake may be low-normal despite iodine loadThionamide (methimazole), beta-blocker; perchlorate where available
Amiodarone, type 2 thyrotoxicosisNormal gland, low or absent vascularity and uptakeGlucocorticoids; amiodarone can often continue if needed for the arrhythmia, decided with cardiology
Amiodarone hypothyroidismHigh TSHLevothyroxine; amiodarone can continue
Checkpoint-inhibitor thyroiditisThyrotoxicosis with low uptake, then hypothyroidism weeks laterBeta-blocker for symptoms, monitor TSH and free T4 every few weeks, levothyroxine when hypothyroid; immunotherapy usually continues
Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow) thyrotoxicosisOlder patient with nodular goiter after contrastBeta-blocker and methimazole

Checkpoint inhibitors: other endocrinopathies

  • Hypophysitis: headache and fatigue, low ACTH and cortisol, often low TSH with low free T4. Start glucocorticoid replacement before levothyroxine, because thyroid hormone speeds cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.
  • Insulin-deficient diabetes: rapid onset, often with DKA, low C-peptide. Treat with insulin; glucocorticoids do not reverse it.
  • Primary adrenalitis is rare; treat with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.

Other drug-related problems

  • SGLT2 inhibitor euglycemic DKA: anion-gap acidosis with ketones and glucose often below 250 mg/dL. Stop the drug, give fluids and an insulin infusion with dextrose. Hold SGLT2 inhibitors before planned surgery (3 days for most agents, 4 days for ertugliflozin) and during acute illness.
  • Antipsychotic hyperprolactinemia: if psychiatric illness allows, switch to a prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole) or add low-dose aripiprazole; check a pregnancy test and consider pituitary imaging if prolactin is very high or there are mass symptoms.
  • Biotin interference: high-dose biotin (hair, skin and nail supplements) interferes with streptavidin-biotin immunoassays, falsely lowering results of sandwich assays (TSH) and falsely raising results of competitive assays (free T4, T3), mimicking hyperthyroidism. Stop biotin for at least 2–3 days and repeat the tests.
  • Testosterone therapy: monitor hematocrit; it suppresses spermatogenesis and should not be used by men trying to conceive.

Exam trap: in suspected central hypothyroidism with possible ACTH deficiency (hypophysitis, pituitary disease), give glucocorticoid before levothyroxine.
